This paper presents CloudRL, a deep reinforcement learning framework for intelligent cloud resource allocation that jointly optimizes resource utilization, Service Level Agreement (SLA) compliance, infrastructure cost, and energy efficiency. CloudRL formulates resource allocation as a continuous-action Markov Decision Process (MDP) and employs a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) agent with a multi-objective reward function that balances competing optimization goals through adaptive weighting. The system observes a high-dimensional state space comprising real-time CPU, memory, GPU, storage I/O, and network utilization metrics alongside workload arrival patterns and SLA parameters, and outputs fine-grained scaling, migration, and configuration actions. We evaluate CloudRL on a production-scale testbed comprising 500 virtual machines processing six diverse workload traces (web serving, batch analytics, machine learning training, video transcoding, database, and microservices) over 30 days. Results demonstrate that CloudRL achieves 88% average resource utilization (compared to 42% for static allocation and 65% for predictive methods), reduces SLA violations by 91.7% (from 12% to 0.98%), decreases infrastructure costs by 37.5%, and lowers energy consumption by 59% compared to static provisioning. CloudRL converges within 3,000 training episodes and adapts to workload distribution shifts within 200 episodes without manual retuning.

title: Super Mean Graph Labeling: A Novel Cryptographic Framework Using Five-Star Graphs with Applications in Secure Communications and Epidemic Modeling
authors: Sudhakar V, Leena S, Anuradha P, DR. Indhumathi R -, Avinash N, Balaji V
abstract: This paper introduces an innovative cryptographic framework based on super mean labeling of five-star graphs K1,V1 ∪ K1,V2 ∪ K1,V3 ∪ K1,V4 ∪ K1,V5, where V1 ≤ V2 ≤ V3 ≤ V4 ≤ V5. We present a comprehensive mathematical foundation for super mean labeling and develop systematic methodologies for encoding messages through carefully constructed graph structures. Three distinct implementation approaches are demonstrated, incorporating computational techniques through C programming for alphabetical mapping, including subtraction-based and division-based numbering schemes. Each approach is thoroughly illustrated with complete message encoding examples, visual cryptography representations, and detailed security analysis. Beyond cryptographic applications, we extend the framework to epidemic modeling, demonstrating how super mean labeling can represent complex disease transmission dynamics in multi-population systems. The epidemic modeling application includes complete mathematical formulations of multi-population SIR models, transmission matrix encoding through graph labeling, and computational implementations for disease surveillance. Our results establish that five-star graphs with super mean labeling provide optimal balance between encoding capacity and structural complexity, offering robust security through multiple layers of mathematical obfuscation. The integration of graph theory with computational algorithms creates a versatile framework applicable to both secure communications and public health informatics.

title: Advancing Post-Cryptographic Schemes Using Number Theoretic Structures: Algorithms, Security, and Real World Implementation
authors: Jency J, Usha A
abstract: Cryptography, a term rooted in Greek that translates to 'secure writing,' encompasses the intricate study of methods employed to encrypt and decrypt information, ensuring secure communication between parties. This fundamental discipline plays a critical role in safeguarding sensitive data from unauthorized access and malicious entities. The process begins with encryption, where plain text, or the original readable information, is transformed into ciphertext through specific algorithms and protocols. This transformation obscures the content, making it unintelligible to anyone who does not possess the appropriate keys or credentials to decode it. Decryption is the complementary process that reverses this transformation, restoring the ciphertext to its original plain text format. This allows authorized users to access the information securely while preventing would-be intruders from deciphering its contents. In addition to these basic principles, modern cryptography incorporates various techniques, such as symmetric and asymmetric encryption, digital signatures, and hash functions, each serving specific purposes in the realm of data protection and secure communication. Overall, cryptography is essential in today's digital landscape, underpinning everything from online banking transactions to secure messaging systems and helping to ensure the integrity and privacy of information exchanged over insecure networks.

title: Magnetic resonance imaging and spatial localized spectroscopy using intermolecular multiple-quantum coherences: techniques and clinical utility for brain
authors: Dan E. Demco, Radu Fechete, Ruben Emanuel Nechifor
abstract: This review is focused on the investigation on brain microstructure using advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and spectroscopy (MRS). These echniques were introduced in the last decades using NMR based on intermolecular multiplequantum coherences (iMQCs), excited and detected in the presence of the long-range dipolar inter-nuclear couplings induced by correlated gradients. The origin of multiple spin echoes and nonlinear coherence transfer echoes based on COSY revamped by asymmetric Z-gradient echo detection (CRAZED) in liquids are discussed using quantum-mechanics formalism. The accent of this review is on the intermolecular zero-quantum coherences (iZQCs) and intermolecular double-quantum coherences (iDQCs) excitation, evolution, and detection in the presence of correlated field gradients using the CRAZED pulse sequences. The applications of this pulse sequence to reduce the effect of inhomogeneous magnetic fields and to increase the image resolution is reviewed in the field of magnetic resonance imaging and localized spectroscopy with the accent on brain investigations. The physics related to the used of CRAZED methods is also addressed to produce fundamentally different contrast than does conventional imaging. The effects of spatial inhomogeneity and temporal instability of the NMR made at ultra-high magnetic field are nearly eliminated using iZQCs, thereby achieving a resolution enhancement. This will open new frontiers in the nonlinear spatial localized NMR spectroscopy and magnetic resonance imaging. The large nuclear magnetization induced by different hyperpolarization methods allows detection of intermolecular multiple-quantum coherences in liquids, for nuclei in low abundance and/or having low gyromagnetic ratio, and even in low density matter like gases.

title: Intelligent detection of adversaries in quantum key distribution-secured IoT networks using machine learning techniques
authors: Dipanwita Debnath, Karri Manoz Kumar Reddy, Saka Satya Sudha, Anuradha Konidena, Vuppuloori Ravi Sekhara Reddy, Nallathambi Srija
journal: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
abstract: The increasing deployment of internet of things (IoT) devices in beyond-fifth-generation (B5G) and sixth-generation (6G) networks introduces significant security challenges due to limited computational and energy resources. Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables secure key establishment; however, malicious interference can compromise key generation and disrupt communication. This study aims to develop a machine learning (ML)-based framework for detecting adversarial interference using final quantum key length without interrupting QKD operation. A hierarchical architecture is proposed, assigning QKD and ML processing to capable IoT controllers and servers while maintaining lightweight sensor operations. A dataset containing 20,000 simulated QKD key-length samples, representing attack-free and attack-affected scenarios, is used to train and evaluate artificial neural network (ANN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) models. Experimental results demonstrate detection performance close to 99%, with ANN achieving substantially lower computational cost than LSTM. The framework is further considered for railway IoT monitoring, integrating fiber-optic QKD links between controllers and a control center with encrypted wireless sensor communication. The findings highlight the potential of final-key-length-based learning for lightweight, non-intrusive attack detection, while identifying synthetic data and single-feature learning as limitations requiring further validation.

title: Clinical risk-aware routing for secure IoMT data in edge-fog-cloud environments
authors: Rayane Moustapha ElRaba'a, Soha Rawas, Ali El‐Zaart
journal: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
abstract: The internet of medical things (IoMT) enables continuous, real-time monitoring of patients through wearable and bedside sensors, but conventional edge-fog-cloud routing strategies optimize only network-centric quality of service (QoS) metrics and ignore the clinical urgency of the transmitted data, creating a safety risk for high-risk patients. This paper proposes fog-aware patient-network scoring (FA-PNS), a continuous, clinical risk-aware routing framework that embeds a normalized patient risk score directly into the routing utility function through an elastic clinical penalty mechanism, allowing routing sensitivity to scale smoothly with patient risk rather than relying on fixed thresholds. FA-PNS is evaluated on a synthetic dataset of 10,000 IoMT patient instances against five baseline routing strategies (latency-based, shortest-path, congestion-aware, weighted multi-metric, and priority-based). Results show that FA-PNS reduces the unsafe routing rate for high-risk patients from 93.33% (latency-based routing) to 3.33%, while improving high-risk patient end-to-end latency by 15.01% compared with priority-based routing (68.91 ms versus 81.08 ms), with all improvements statistically significant (paired t-test, p

title: Implementation of a secure digital data exchange framework based on post-quantum cryptography
authors: Nhu-Quynh Luc, Duc-Huy Quach, Thanh-Long Le-Nguyen, Duy-Phuong Nguyen
journal: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
abstract: Quantum computing threatens Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA)- and elliptic-curve-based data exchange, motivating practical post-quantum cryptography (PQC). This study implements a cross-platform file-exchange framework using Kyber-1024 for key encapsulation mechanism (KEM)-based session-key establishment, Falcon-1024 detached signatures, and advanced encryption standard (AES)-256-cipher block chaining mode (CBC) for bulk encryption. Evaluation covered an IEEE 802.11ac Linux/Windows testbed (1,000–40,365 KiB) and controlled single-host transmission control protocol (TCP)-loopback runs up to 102,400 KiB. The three reported Linux-to-Linux wireless session-key-establishment times averaged 25.26 ms (approximately 25.3 ms); encrypting 4,352 KiB in 29.8 ms yielded 142.6 MiB/s. Inspection of captured packets revealed no plaintext file content or session-key material in the application payloads, and a forged file/signature pair was rejected. These results support implementation feasibility on commodity hardware within the tested workflow, but they do not establish authenticated key exchange, active man-in-the-middle (MITM) resistance, metadata confidentiality, or traffic-analysis resistance.

title: Dual-stage autoencoder and density clustering for unsupervised cloud intrusion detection
authors: Sant Kumar Maurya, Tamilarasi Karuppiah, Sunil Kumar, Gaurav Vinchurkar, Praveen Kumar Gupta, Anubhav Kumar
journal: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
abstract: Cloud intrusion detection remains challenging because modern network traffic is high-dimensional, highly imbalanced, and continuously evolving. Although autoencoders and density-based clustering have been applied independently for intrusion detection, directly clustering the learned latent space often reduces the separation between benign and malicious traffic, particularly for minority attacks. This paper presents a dual-stage unsupervised intrusion detection approach that combines latent representation learning with anomaly-filtered density clustering. A dual-function autoencoder is first trained using benign traffic to learn compact latent representations while identifying anomalous flows through reconstruction error. Instead of clustering the complete latent space, only the latent representations of detected anomalies are forwarded to density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) for attack grouping. This anomaly-filtered clustering strategy reduces the influence of dominant benign traffic and improves the discrimination of attack patterns in the latent space. The proposed method was evaluated on the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 benchmark dataset containing diverse cloud network attacks. Experimental results achieved 99.46% anomaly detection accuracy and 98.81% multiclass attack classification accuracy using a 21-dimensional latent representation. Improved clustering quality was further confirmed by a Silhouette score of 0.9859 and a Davies-Bouldin index (DBI) of 0.0093. The proposed pipeline provides an effective unsupervised solution for cloud intrusion detection without requiring attack labels during model training.

title: Analysis of the impact of natural language selection in large language models on energy consumption
authors: Tomasz Szymczyk, Marcin Badurowicz, Janusz Kozak
journal: Advances in Science and Technology – Research Journal
abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference is computationally intensive, yet the extent to which the interaction language affects energy consumption remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates whether inference energy consumption varies across six European languages: Polish, English, German, French, Spanish, and Russian. Three open-weight models, Llama3.1-8b, Gemma-3-12b, and Qwen2.5-14b, were evaluated using ten semantically equivalent prompts, each translated into the six languages and repeated three times. Experiments were conducted on a workstation-class server equipped with an AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT GPU and the Ollama inference framework. Whole-system power consumption was measured using a calibrated HIOKI PW3337 power meter, and energy efficiency was expressed as energy per generated token (EPT). Mean EPT varied substantially among models: Llama3.1-8b consumed 6.43 J/token, Qwen2.5-14b 10.23 J/token, and Gemma-3-12b 10.87 J/token. Kruskal–Wallis tests identified statistically significant between-language differences only for Llama3.1-8b; no significant differences were found for Qwen2.5-14b or Gemma-3-12b. However, regression analysis for Llama3.1-8b showed that response length was the dominant predictor of EPT, as fixed inference overhead was amortized over longer outputs. The findings indicate that apparent language-dependent differences in inference energy are driven primarily by generated-output length rather than by language itself. Energy efficiency also depends strongly on model architecture, tokenizer behavior, and inference implementation, highlighting the importance of response-length control and whole-system measurement in Green AI benchmarking.

title: AI-assisted design and control of a landsman converter for electric vehicle charging applications with advanced power factor correction
authors: Sivaprasad Kollati, R. A. Archana, Tadanki Vijay Muni, Ramoju Bheema Sankaram, S. Subramanya Sarma, D. Silas Stephen, Kartik Anilkumar, K. Suriyakrishnaan
journal: International Journal of Power Electronics and Drive Systems/International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering
abstract: The burgeoning electric vehicle (EV) industry necessitates cutting-edge solutions to improve the efficiency and sustainability of EV charging systems. This paper presents an innovative Landsman converter design tailored for EV charging applications, incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) to achieve effective power factor correction (PFC). The integration of AI into the converter's control strategy enhances its ability to optimize operational performance, ensuring a high-power factor, minimizing harmonic distortion, and boosting energy efficiency throughout the charging process. The study develops a sophisticated simulation model of the Landsman converter using MATLAB/Simulink, wherein AI algorithms are employed to dynamically adjust the converter's operation. This approach enables the system to adapt to varying load conditions and input voltages, demonstrating superior performance in terms of power factor correction and overall efficiency. The simulation results underscore the potential of combining AI with power electronics to elevate EV charging technology, offering significant advancements in creating smarter, more reliable, and efficient charging infrastructures. This research highlights the transformative impact of AI on enhancing power electronics designs, paving the way for more sustainable and effective solutions in the rapidly evolving EV sector.

title: Hybrid SNGNN–BKOA framework for intelligent congestion management in renewable-integrated power systems
authors: Venkateswarlu Tata, Nagamani Tenali, Maddukuri Venkata Ramesh, Kotikala Narayana Rao, Manam Ravindra, Jampani Satish Babu
journal: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
abstract: The rapid integration of renewable energy sources (RES), such as wind and solar, introduces significant variability and uncertainty in modern power systems, which often leads to transmission congestion and operational inefficiencies. This paper proposes a hybrid congestion management framework that combines a similarity-navigated graph neural network (SNGNN) with the black-winged kite optimization algorithm (BKOA). The SNGNN model captures complex spatial relationships within the power network to accurately forecast load demand, while BKOA optimizes congestion mitigation by coordinating generator rescheduling and energy storage system (ESS) operations. The proposed framework was evaluated through MATLAB simulations under different renewable penetration levels. Results demonstrate that the SNGNN–BKOA approach achieves superior performance compared with benchmark algorithms such as grey wolf optimizer (GWO) and salp swarm algorithm (SSA). The proposed method reduces system power loss to 48.4 MW, achieves a forecasting RMSE of 0.164%, and lowers congestion mitigation costs to $5800.09/h at 10% renewable penetration and $6823.71/h at 40% penetration. These results indicate that the proposed hybrid learning–optimization framework improves grid stability, reduces operational cost, and enhances decision-making for congestion management in renewable-dominated smart grids.

title: A hybrid Inception-attention VGG and quantum variational learning framework for scalable healthcare data analytics
authors: K Prasanna, Gaddam Venu Gopal, Pramod Kumar Irlapati, A. Muthukrishnan, Divvela Srinivasa Rao, Thotakura Venkata Sai Krishna, Choutupalli Lavanya Susanna
journal: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
abstract: The rapid expansion of clinical data requires analytical frameworks capable of handling high-dimensional, heterogeneous, and noisy medical information. Classical deep learning models provide strong feature extraction capabilities but are often computationally intensive and prone to scalability limitations. Conversely, quantum machine learning (QML) offers enhanced representational capacity but suffers from hardware constraints and noise sensitivity. To address these shortcomings, this paper proposes a hybrid deep learning–quantum processing architecture integrating an Inception-attention-based visual geometry group (VGG) network for multiscale feature extraction with a quantum variational classifier (QVC) optimized using parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs). Clinical data from the MIMIC-III dataset undergo min–max normalization, multi-resolution convolutional feature extraction, and quantum-enhanced classification. Experiments demonstrate superior performance compared to classical support vector machine (SVM), quantum support vector machines (QSVM), quantum kernel support vector machine (QKSVM), quantum variational support vector machine (QVSVM), and quantum variational kernel support vector machine (QVKSVM) models. The proposed framework achieves 98.79% accuracy, 98.67% precision, 98.15% recall, and 98.88% F1-score, representing a subtle 0.3% improvement over existing quantum-assisted hybrid models. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed hybrid framework within the adopted classical–quantum simulation environment and motivate further validation on real near-term quantum hardware.

title: Deploying enhanced security for blockchain MFA wireless virtual-key access management for industrial frontiers
authors: Andrew Okonji Eboka, Fidelis Obukohwo Aghware, Margaret Dumebi Okpor, Bridget Ogheneovo Malasowe, Ejaita Abugor Okpako, Arnold Adimabua Ojugo, Reuben Akporube Abere, Amaka Patience Binitie
journal: International Journal of Informatics and Communication Technology (IJ-ICT)
abstract: The increased adoption of automated devices and its utilization to advance data processing in many facets of societal tasks and demand operations has continued to birth accompanying security challenges. Physical infrastructures today integrates within them automated units to upscale traditional issues. The recent proliferation of automated door access with innovative embedded units employs a centralized design with single-factor authentication, which has proven inefficient for safeguarding restricted environments. Other challenges of data corruption, theft, mishandle of user credentials, all of which can be compromised due to its single point of access control. This study advances enhanced access security for virtual key door infrastructure via a blockchain-MFA strategy. It implements secure, scalable access control with a 3-layered framework of PIN + RFID + Biometric, validated using smart contracts on a blockchain network. The results demonstrated improvements in security, transparency, and auditability compared to traditional door access control, especially against adversarial attacks from single-point failures and credential vulnerabilities. Our prototype unit demonstrates 3-factor authentication for improved security that ensures forensic traceability of every authentication attempt, making it a viable solution for institutions with high-security needs.

title: Beyond Qubit Count: A Comparative Review of Quantum Chip Architectures, Error Correction, and the Path to Fault-Tolerant Computing
authors: Sairaj Dalvi, Suyog Salvi, Tanmay Patil, Prof. Mrs. Ravina Khachane
journal: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
abstract: Quantum processors are often compared by the number of physical qubits they contain. That number, however, does not by itself indicate whether a processor can execute a useful computation reliably. Qubit coherence, gate and measurement fidelity, connectivity, control infrastructure, fabrication yield, and the overhead of quantum error correction all influence practical capability. This paper presents a structured comparative review of six major quantum-computing modalities: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photonic systems, silicon-spin qubits, neutral atoms, and topological approaches. It examines their physical implementations, operational strengths, engineering constraints, and prospects for scaling. Particular attention is given to surface-code error correction and the 105-qubit Willow processor result reported by Google Quantum AI, which demonstrated below-threshold surface-code memory and a logical-error suppression factor of 2.14 ± 0.02 when code distance increased by two. The paper also considers cryogenic control, wiring, modular interconnects, fabrication variability, real-time decoding, and the Indian National Quantum Mission. The review finds that progress towards fault tolerance is best assessed through logical performance and system-level engineering rather than physical-qubit count alone. No modality currently removes the need to address scaling overhead, reliable operations, and application-level advantage

title: QS-ENN: Dataset-dependent Quantum Resampling for Imbalanced Medical Data under Exact-statevector Simulation
authors: Agustinus Eko Setiawan, Abdul Syukur, Moch Arief Soeleman, Supriadi Rustad
journal: International journal of intelligent engineering and systems
abstract: Existing quantum oversampling methods do not jointly coordinate borderline allocation, geodesic synthesis, and protective cleaning within a consistent quantum geometry.This study proposes QS-ENN (Quantum SMOTE-Edited Nearest Neighbor), integrating fidelity-guided safe-level seed allocation, Fubini-Study geodesic synthesis, and Protective Quantum-ENN.Ten medical datasets were evaluated using fold-isolated preprocessing, target-leakage exclusion, exact-statevector fidelity simulation, Quantum-SMOTEV2 comparison, and equal-budget nested validation.QS-ENN achieved its clearest improvement on HCV (F1=0.554),gaining +0.085 over QKNN+SMOTE-ENN, +0.117 over Quantum-SMOTE, and +0.060 over Quantum-SMOTEV2.It also significantly outperformed both quantum oversamplers on PIMA and Breast Cancer, whereas Quantum-SMOTEV2 performed better on Frankfurt Diabetes and Obesity.Typhoid was excluded from comparative claims because AUC=0.495 indicated chance-level discrimination.Cross-dataset ablation revealed component-level sign reversals, while geometry descriptors provided no reliable predeployment rule.Overall, QS-ENN is a reproducible algorithmic framework whose effectiveness remains dependent on dataset and representation characteristics rather than demonstrating universal superiority.

title: Content-adaptive Multi-channel Hybrid Quantum-classical Block-wise Optimization for Robust Image Watermarking
authors: Nova Rijati, Aris Marjuni, Sudipta Kr Ghosal, Aditya Kumar Sahu, Deshinta Arrova Dewi, De Rosal Ignatius Moses Setiadi
journal: International journal of intelligent engineering and systems
abstract: The rapid growth of digital image distribution necessitates robust watermarking techniques to protect ownership and ensure data integrity.This paper proposes a content-adaptive hybrid quantum-classical watermarking framework that integrates local adaptive modeling and global optimization.The method employs Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) and Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to provide a stable embedding domain.Local texture features are extracted from image blocks and mapped using a trained Parameterized Quantum Circuit (PQC) to determine adaptive embedding strength.In parallel, Quantum-Inspired Annealing (QIA) is used to optimize the selection of DCT coefficient positions globally.A multi-channel embedding strategy is further incorporated to enhance robustness.Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high imperceptibility (PSNR > 47 dB, SSIM ≈ 0.99) and strong robustness against the evaluated attacks, while remaining competitive with existing methods.The proposed framework provides a hybrid quantum-classical approach to image watermarking and represents a process innovation by integrating adaptive quantum learning with global coefficient-position optimization for robust multimedia copyright protection.

title: Hybrid Supervised-unsupervised Learning Framework for Financial Data Analysis Enhanced by Quantum-inspired Computing
authors: Praneeth Reddy Amudala Puchakayala, Poonam Ghule, Vijay Vaswani, Jeevith S H
journal: International journal of intelligent engineering and systems
abstract: Financial time-series analysis poses some difficulties, due to the non-stationarity of data, its distribution is heavy-tailed, the regime structure in financial time-series is latent, and there are few labelled training signals available.These models are highly sensitive to unexpected trade-offs and limited out-of-distribution generalisation, and unsupervised models, on their own, are unable to directly inform tradeable decisions.This paper proposes a framework named Quantum-Inspired Hybrid Supervised-Unsupervised Learning (QIHSL) consisting of three tightly-integrated modules: (1) Quantum-Inspired Feature Transformation (QFT) module that maps the financial features into amplitudeand phase-encoded qubit-state analogues, and generates the cross-feature interaction terms inspired by entanglement;(2) Quantum-Inspired K-Means (QI-KMeans) clustering module that uses the quantum fidelity based distance metric to learn the regime (bull, bear, sideways) of the data in an unsupervised manner; and (3) a Quantum-Inspired Support Vector Machine (QI-SVM) regime-gated ensemble for robust and regime-aware return-direction prediction with QI-SVMs that specialise in predicting the return direction in different market regimes.The experiments on a comprehensive benchmark dataset of 4,950 synthetic daily observations from the S&P 500 index, used to capture the statistical properties of equity markets, namely Student-t distributed returns (ν = 5), three-state regime switching and nineteen technical indicators, show that QIHSL achieves an accuracy of 0.4913, a precision of 0.5538, a recall of 0.2588, an F1-score of 0.3527 and an AUC of 0.5029 on the hold-out test set, outperforming the baseline SVM by 5.92 percentage points in precision.It represents the best of all six comparison methods (Table 2) and for all the architectures in the matched-condition comparison (Table 7) is an advantage (not a finding) of precision for two instances of the simulation and does not necessarily mean that they are more likely to forecast than others.The controlled ablation study (Table 3) also shows that a component-level benefit for quantum-inspired feature enrichment can be measured by the QFT module's accuracy of +2.0 pp and F1-score of +11.9 pp over the SVM baseline (A2 vs. A1).Five-fold stratified cross validation gives a stability of AUC = 0.4987 ± 0.0095.An ablation study shows that the QFT module contributes the largest single-step accuracy gain (+2.0 pp) and F1-score gain (+11.9 pp over A1); adding regime gating further improves accuracy (+0.95 pp) but reduces F1 (-0.0786) and AUC (-0.0123) relative to QFT alone.The reported AUC (around 0.5) is at chance level, and no pairwise McNemar comparison is significant at alpha = 0.05 (the smallest p = 0.2433), which is consistent with the almost efficient nature of the synthetic benchmark.Combined, results show no statistically relevant predictive value for the synthetic benchmark.The most interesting aspect of QIHSL is its highest precision (0.5538) of all methods compared, which could have some relevance to conservative trading, but not to proven practical forecast effectiveness.

title: MQDA-Net: A Quantum-enhanced Dual-branch Framework for Unified Brain Tumor Segmentation, Classification and Structured Radiology Report Generation
authors: subia salma, Sanjeev C. Lingareddy, S. Shilpashree, Vineet Kumar
journal: International journal of intelligent engineering and systems
abstract: Automated brain tumor analysis from multi-parametric MRI is typically split into three separately solved problems: volumetric segmentation, tumor-type classification and radiology report generation.The few unified systems chain these stages rather than optimizing them jointly, and inherit the weaknesses of every link: slice-level segmenters that discard volumetric context, classification heads carrying tens of millions of parameters that overfit small neuro-oncology cohorts, static knowledge graphs that cannot reason from image evidence, and report generators whose output barely overlaps clinician text.We propose MQDA-Net, which integrates all three tasks in one architecture, each pathway optimized on the cohort carrying its annotations and coupled to the others through shared representations and explicit conditioning.A three-dimensional encoder with block-level Multi-Scale Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (MSASPP) widens the bottleneck receptive field.A Dual-Branch Discriminative Decoder couples a coarse binary localization branch to a fine-grained semantic branch through cross-attention, injecting an explicit localization prior into sub-region assignment.A twelve-qubit variational classification head (parameterized U3 rotations, controlled-Z entanglement and Pauli-X readout) replaces the conventional stacked classifier, reducing classifier parameters from 67.2 M to 7.3 M. A dynamic image-grounded knowledge graph, built per case from segmentation masks and MNI atlas co-registration and refined by a Graph Attention Network, conditions a Q-Formerprojected LoRA-adapted Llama 3.2 11B Vision-Instruct backbone that emits structured reports carrying volumetric measurements, anatomical localization and BT-RADS risk stratification.On BraTS 2023, MQDA-Net reaches mean Dice 0.91 and IoU 0.84; on the harder BraTS 2024 post-treatment cohort the framework reaches 79.85 % Dice, exceeding a self-supervised specialist baseline by 4.61 points.Classification accuracy reaches 99.72 % on the Nickparvar composite benchmark, and report BLEU improves from 0.068 to 0.170 with ROUGE-L F1 rising from 0.0018 to 0.068.Differences against published values for the closest prior unified framework are reported descriptively; no matched statistical comparison is claimed.

title: Fourier Positioned-INR MobileNetV1 Fusion Framework for Maternal-fetal Plane Classification
authors: Chaitali Haldankar ., H. P. Rajani
journal: International journal of intelligent engineering and systems
abstract: Accurate classification of maternal-fetal ultrasound planes is an arduous and challenging task owing to lowresolution image quality, anatomical variability, maternal-fetal movements, and sonographers' expertise.This leads to misclassification of maternal-fetal US planes, causing anomalies to go unnoticed.This study presents a retrospective model development and internal validation process through a lightweight Fourier-encoded coordinate implicit neural representation (INR)-CNN framework for six-class maternal-fetal ultrasound plane classification.The framework combines image-dependent convolutional features extracted by an ImageNet-pretrained MobileNetV1 backbone with a shared positional feature field learned from normalized two-dimensional coordinates.Six-frequency sinusoidal Fourier encoding expands each coordinate pair into a 26-dimensional representation, which is processed by coordinatewise 1 × 1 convolutional layers.The resulting positional feature map is spatially aligned with the projected MobileNetV1 feature map and fused through channel-wise concatenation and a 1 × 1 convolutional projection.Global average pooling and a regularized softmax classifier are subsequently used to classify fetal abdomen, fetal brain, fetal femur, fetal thorax, maternal cervix, and other ultrasound images.The model was evaluated using 12,400 images from 1,792 patients in the publicly available Fetal Planes DB dataset.The dataset was divided at the patient level into training, validation, and test sets containing 10,203 images from 1,433 patients, 1,062 images from 179 patients, and 1,135 images from 180 patients, respectively.No patient overlap was observed among the three partitions.Performance was assessed using patient-level stratified ten-fold cross-validation with identical locked folds across the ablation models, followed by evaluation on an untouched patient-independent test cohort.The proposed Fourier-INR fusion model achieved an accuracy of 90.16 ± 1.04% under ten-fold cross-validation and an accuracy of 91.10% with a macro F1-score of 88.53% on the untouched test cohort.The proposed model outperformed the MobileNetV1 baseline on the untouched test cohort, increasing accuracy from 90.57% to 91.10%.These findings demonstrate that integrating a shared multi-frequency positional representation with image-dependent Mo-bileNetV1 features provides a modest performance improvement over the corresponding CNN baseline while retaining a lightweight classification architecture.While external and multicentre validation is required before clinical deployment, this lightweight framework holds strong potential to aid automated prenatal workflows and clinical decision support.

title: Spintronics in Lead‐Free Hybrid Perovskites: Mechanisms, Materials, and Prospects for Room‐Temperature Devices
authors: Ying Lu, DeYan Huo, JieYing Wang, Zhe Zhang, ChenXi Yu, Yuzhen Zhao, Zongcheng Miao
abstract: Lead‐halide perovskites demonstrate room‐temperature spintronic functionality, yet their reliance on Pb‐containing lattices raises environmental concerns. Any replacement must be assessed at the composition and device‐stack levels. This Perspective argues that advancing lead‐free spintronics requires decoupling spin functionality from Pb‐containing lattices, rather than eliminating heavy‐element spin‐orbit coupling. We distinguish spin responses rooted in bulk or local symmetry from interface‐enabled injection, conversion, and readout. We compare Sn‐, Cu‐, and Bi‐based materials and assess device architectures. We examine interface engineering as a route to separate spin‐selective interfacial functions from the primary charge‐transport pathway. This separation may reduce the transport penalty imposed by bulky chiral ligands, but it does not by itself establish spin filtering or preserve carrier mobility. We distinguish direct lead‐free measurements from Pb‐based comparison systems and treat polarization‐sensitive photodetection as an adjacent optoelectronic function rather than evidence of spin‐resolved readout. This transition requires controlling defect‐driven electronic and ionic backgrounds and standardizing metrology to distinguish genuine interfacial spin phenomena from thermal artifacts. This analysis yields three testable requirements: identify the microscopic origin of a spin response, specify the role of the interface, and verify spin transport or conversion using mechanism‐specific controls and an independent spin‐sensitive observable.

title: Energy-filtered readout preserves gap-enhanced sensing in interacting quantum dots
authors: Shirwan Abdullah
abstract: A small excitation gap makes a quantum dot a sensitive probe of a weak electric field, but the charge detector reading it can also excite it. We calculate how much of this enhancement survives continuous readout for two interacting electrons tuned through a confinement-driven crossover in a gate-defined dot. The probe is a few-level system read by a weakly coupled linear detector, with second-order transition rates and information from the mean detector current, for gaps up to a few hundred microelectronvolts, couplings up to 50 µeV and temperatures up to 100 mK. The outcome depends on the detector's energy structure, not only its noise. A quantum point contact measures more strongly at higher bias but, once the bias energy exceeds the gap, also excites the probe; when this back-action dominates the probe's relaxation, the optimised information rate grows only as the inverse of the gap. A sensor quantum dot with a narrow level instead reaches full strength at a bias below the gap, where a non-interacting detector cannot excite it at zero temperature. This energy-filtered readout keeps the inverse-square gap dependence of the quantum Fisher information down to gaps comparable to the detector's level width or ten times the thermal energy. At the tested operating points, higher probe states change the sensitivities by up to 6% and the exponents by up to 0.06; coherence corrections to the populations and transduced signal are negligible, and any gain from the full detector record is unresolved within 1–2% numerical uncertainty. Under the same conditions the interacting pair gives about three times the information rate of a single electron with the same gap and detector, for contact and Coulomb-type interactions alike. The different gap dependences and optimal biases of the two detectors can be tested by bias and gate sweeps on charge-sensed double dots.

title: Memory-dependent operating windows for photonic teleportation from a laser-driven spin–photon interface
authors: Mukhtar Y. Y. Abdalla, Naglaa Mohammed, Osman Osman, Ines Hilali Jaghdam, Muntasir Suhail, Muhammad Javed
abstract: Generating entangled photons from a laser-driven spin provides a promising resource for quantum communication, but their usefulness can depend on how the surrounding nuclear environment evolves during photon generation. We investigate a spin–photon interface driven by finite laser pulses while retaining nuclear-spin dynamics across successive emission cycles. Measurements on the intermediate photons produce conditional endpoint states, whose entanglement, Bell correlations, teleportation fidelity, and expected detection rates are evaluated. By comparing dynamically evolving, frozen-field, and reset nuclear environments, we find that simplified noise models can predict different operating windows for useful teleportation. In particular, the frozen-field approximation may overestimate performance under the conditions studied. Optical branching, imperfect feedforward, and nuclear-register size further constrain these windows. The results establish a task-oriented framework for evaluating photonic resources while highlighting the need for accurate environmental modeling and device-specific calibration.

title: Smart soft matter: from high-resolution fabrication to physical intelligence
authors: Hanxu Chen, Mingchao Zhang
abstract: Soft matter, characterized by flexibility, biocompatibility, and adaptability, has been widely explored in cutting-edge technological domains, including microrobotics, biomedicine, and wearable devices. Integration with high-resolution additive manufacturing, namely three-dimensional printing, enables the bottom-up construction of complex micro-/nanostructures from a broad palette of soft materials with unprecedented spatial resolution and design freedom. Moreover, the realization of physical intelligence in soft matter requires the ability to encode structural, chemical, mechanical, and functional information into materials across multiple length scales. Herein, we first discuss the intrinsic resolution constraints of representative high-resolution fabrication techniques. Then we discuss the critical elements of physical intelligence enabled by high-resolution fabrication. Building on this, we explore the remaining challenges arising from the fabrication process and material properties. Finally, we outline the future development directions of smart soft matter with programmable physical intelligence. This perspective highlights high-resolution fabrication as a critical bridge between soft matter structuring and physical intelligence.

title: Enhancing quantum metrology with high-order Fisher information and experiments
authors: Xin-Zhu Liu, Junli Jiang, Yan-Han Yang, L Zhao, Xiaomin Yang, Shao‐Ming Fei, Ming-Xing Luo
abstract: Fisher information plays a central role in statistics and quantum metrology, providing the basis for the celebrated Cramér–Rao bound. In this work, we introduce a new information measure based on higher-order Fisher information and show that it naturally leads to a generalized uncertainty relation for parameter estimation, which can be regarded as an extension of the Cramér–Rao bound. As an application, we analyze the case of quantum phase estimation and compare our theoretical bounds with the well-known established hierarchical bounds. Finally, we experimentally validate the proposed framework using a photonic platform.

title: Architectures of Sovereign AI in the Neural Age: Epistemic Agency, Managed Interdependence, and an Empirical Stress-Test of the 2027 Horizon
authors: Syed Muntasir Mamun
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical formalization, comparative institutional analysis, and late-2026 empirical stress-test of operational doctrines for sovereign artificial intelligence (AI), synthesizing and critically extending the KSCCN corpus developed by Syed Muntasir Mamun. Rejecting both territorial autarky and passive absorption into planetary platform monopolies, the study conceptualizes AI sovereignty as the sustained capacity of a political community to retain autonomous control over the epistemic and ontological foundations of its strategic existence. Across seven interlocking domains—local capability formation, enterprise resilience, privacy-preserving cross-border collaboration, regulatory coherence, innovation safeguards and cognitive protection, cross-jurisdictional accountability, and regional shared infrastructure—the analysis evaluates the Triple-Lock Architecture (binding material, civic, and public triads), Dual-Core Fractal Statecraft, and Sovereign Interoperability in dialogue with contesting paradigms, including open-weight maximalism, European regulatory sovereignty, Chinese vertical state control, data-colonialism critiques, and Hakkı Tan's ontopolitical theory of the Onopticon. Grounded in market concentration telemetry, small language model (SLM) and distributed training benchmarks, cryptographic attack surfaces, and enacted statutes as of November 2026 across the European Union, United States, China, India, Southeast Asia, and Africa, the empirical audit establishes two core findings alongside three structural caveats. First, capital-light pathways—combining parameter-efficient fine-tuning, Governance-Aware Retriever middleware, low-communication training, and modular Digital Public Infrastructure—offer a technically viable "Third Way" for middle powers and Global South polities facing an estimated 580-fold fiscal asymmetry against US hyperscalers, yet remain highly vulnerable to execution lags, agent-runtime lock-in, and authoritarian co-optation. Second, stress-testing the KSCCN 2027 horizon forecast strongly corroborates its trajectories regarding agentic proliferation, compute chokepoints, and statutory cognitive safeguards, while refuting its projection of a hardware "Q-Day" around August 2027: late-2026 fault-tolerant hardware (48 small-code logical qubits) remains an order of magnitude or more below RSA-2048 factoring requirements, even though collapsing theoretical qubit overheads and active Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later exposure validate immediate architectural migration toward crypto-agile, post-quantum signed AI memory. KSCCN article, Series on Critical AI and Digital Sovereignty Studies, 26 November 2026 (44 pages, 16 figures, 6 tables, 205 references). Full-colour expanded research edition and empirical stress-test of the KSCCN Teaching Note Architectures of Sovereign AI in the Neural Age: Epistemic Agency, Managed Interdependence, and the 2027 Horizon (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24547226). Draws on Fractal Statecraft under Permanent Systemic Instability (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24298608), Cognitive and Semantic Sovereignty as the New Westphalian Pillar (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24298653), The Algorithmic Leviathan as Constitutional Form, Volume II (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24299263), Sovereign AI for Jute (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24218888), Governing AI Without Governing Speech (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24239711) and Sovereign AI in the Developing Global South (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23543853).

title: Quantum Search Identifies Shared Connections in Lung Cancer Gene Networks
authors: inquantio
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: By comparing 28,390 regulatory interactions inferred from genomic and gene-expression data from lung cancer patients, the researchers identified 4,943 shared connections between two sample sets within the same cohort using quantum circuit simulations, matching the results of classical computation. In a separate comparison involving 7,063 regulatory interactions from two patient cohorts, the researchers identified 24 shared connections. They also tested the core search procedure on a real IBM quantum processor using a reduced 11-qubit circuit. The reported 100% accuracy in large-scale simulations refers to detecting matching connections in previously inferred networks. It does not represent lung cancer diagnostic accuracy or demonstrate faster end-to-end processing than classical computers. [Quantum Biology Society] Understanding lung cancer requires examining not only which genes have changed but also how different genes interact with one another. When certain regions of DNA are amplified or deleted in cancer cells, the expression levels of other genes may also change. These alterations can propagate through complex networks of molecular regulatory relationships. Multi-omics analysis integrates different types of molecular information, such as genomic and transcriptomic data, to represent these relationships as gene regulatory networks (GRNs). A major challenge is identifying connections that consistently appear across large networks constructed from different patient populations. When statistical stability is evaluated through bootstrapping, a procedure that repeatedly resamples data, the number of required network comparisons and the computational burden increase further. Abdul Mannan Kitab and Yiming Zeng of Binghamton University in the United States, Qing Ye of Sostos Inc., and Nancy Lan Guo, who is affiliated with both institutions, developed QuBIN, a quantum computing-based pipeline designed to address this search problem. The researchers designed quantum circuits based on Grover's search algorithm to identify overlapping connections in lung cancer gene regulatory networks. They evaluated the approach using large-scale quantum circuit simulations and experiments on an actual quantum processor. Nancy Lan Guo served as the corresponding author. The study was published online on November 16, 2026, in npj Genomic Medicine. The paper has undergone peer review but is currently available as an accepted Article in Press. Its final bibliographic information and some editorial details may change when the Version of Record is published. ■ Conserved Connections Across Patient Cohorts Matter More Than Individual Genes The central task addressed in this study was not searching individual gene sequences or discovering new regulatory networks from scratch. Instead, the researchers investigated how to identify common regulatory relationships between networks that had already been inferred from biological data. They used DNA copy number variation (CNV) and gene-expression measurements from patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Copy number variation occurs when a region of DNA is present in more or fewer copies than usual. For example, an increase in the copy number of one gene may be statistically associated with increased or decreased expression of another gene. The researchers represented statistically supported directional relationships between these molecular variables as connections, or edges, within gene regulatory networks. These connections had previously been constructed using a framework known as Prediction Logic Boolean Implication Networks (PLBINs). PLBINs identify relationships between molecular variables by evaluating implication rules and their statistical support. For example, if increased DNA copy number of one gene is repeatedly associated with increased expression of another gene, the relationship may be retained as a candidate regulatory interaction when it satisfies predefined statistical criteria. Each connection contains information about the implication-rule type, source gene, target gene, and regulatory direction. However, such a connection does not necessarily demonstrate that the source gene directly causes the observed change in the target gene. The relationships are inferred from molecular data and require additional biological investigation before direct causal mechanisms can be established. The researchers performed two types of network comparisons. The first was an intra-cohort comparison using the publicly available NSCLC dataset GSE31800. This dataset included 271 tumor samples, of which 49 had corresponding gene-expression measurements. The researchers compared two sets of regulatory connections derived from these sample groups. One contained 21,363 edges, while the other contained 7,027 edges. Together, the two sets comprised 28,390 regulatory interactions. Importantly, these were not completely independent patient cohorts. The smaller group of 49 samples was nested within the larger GSE31800 cohort. The second analysis involved an inter-cohort comparison between GSE31800 and an independent NSCLC patient cohort, GSE28582. For this comparison, the researchers examined selected subnetworks associated with a previously investigated seven-gene prognostic signature. The two subnetworks contained 2,014 and 5,049 regulatory interactions, respectively, giving a combined total of 7,063 edges. An interaction was considered conserved between cohorts only when its implication-rule type, source gene, target gene, and regulatory direction matched. Identifying such shared connections can help researchers prioritize molecular relationships for subsequent biomarker investigations. A relationship that appears repeatedly in different patient datasets may be more useful for follow-up research than one identified in only a single dataset. However, recurrence across cohorts does not automatically establish clinical significance or biological causality. The purpose of QuBIN was to improve the computational search for these shared relationships, rather than independently validate their biological functions. ■ The Quantum Circuit Searches for Matching Connections Rather Than Building New Networks The first step in QuBIN is converting each regulatory connection into binary information that can be compared within a quantum circuit. The researchers represented each connection using 33 bits. Of these, 3 bits encoded the regulatory rule type, 15 bits identified the source gene, and another 15 bits identified the target gene. This representation preserved the information needed to determine whether two connections referred to the same regulatory relationship. The researchers then designed a quantum oracle that compared pairs of connections from different networks. A quantum oracle is a component of a quantum algorithm that determines whether a candidate satisfies the conditions of a search problem. In this study, the oracle used exclusive OR (XOR) operations to compare the binary fields of two regulatory connections. An XOR operation returns zero when two compared bits are identical. Therefore, when all the relevant fields of two connections matched, the oracle could identify the pair as a shared regulatory interaction. The corresponding quantum state was marked for amplification by Grover's search algorithm. For intra-cohort comparisons in which all connections within a batch shared the same source gene, the researchers omitted the redundant comparison of that field. This simplified the quantum circuit without changing the matching conditions for the relevant data. Grover's algorithm differs from a conventional sequential search. Instead of examining possible answers one at a time, it uses quantum superposition and interference to increase the probability of measuring states corresponding to valid solutions. The process can be compared to searching a library. Rather than opening every book in sequence, the algorithm progressively increases the probability of selecting books that satisfy the search criteria. However, this is only an analogy. The algorithm does not literally inspect every connection simultaneously and immediately reveal all correct answers. It uses quantum operations to amplify the probability amplitudes of marked states, after which measurements provide candidate results. The researchers divided the large regulatory networks into small batches and applied quantum searches to the individual batch pairs. The results were then collected and combined. This approach differs fundamentally from loading tens of thousands of regulatory interactions into a single quantum computer and searching the entire dataset at once. For the large-scale evaluations, the researchers did not execute the complete circuits on physical quantum hardware. Instead, they used matrix product state (MPS) tensor network simulations running on classical high-performance computing infrastructure. MPS is a mathematical representation that can efficiently simulate certain quantum states when their entanglement structure remains sufficiently constrained. This makes it possible to simulate quantum circuits that would require impractically large memory if represented using full quantum state vectors. The researchers used Qiskit and its MPS simulation backend to evaluate the circuits. For the intra-cohort comparison, the networks were divided into batches containing eight edges each. The corresponding circuit contained 90 qubits. For the inter-cohort comparison, the researchers used batches of four edges and a 104-qubit circuit. These qubit counts describe the sizes of the simulated quantum circuits. They do not mean that the full 90-qubit or 104-qubit experiments were executed on real quantum processors. title: Predicting and Interpreting Quantum Circuit Reliability: An Integrated Machine Learning and XAI Framework
authors: Duong Van Hieu
abstract: Quantum computing promises exponential advantages for classically intractable problems but remains severely bottlenecked by hardware noise.Accurately predicting quantum circuit reliability prior to execution is crucial for effective compilation and error mitigation, yet exact fidelity estimation is computationally prohibitive.While recent machine learning (ML) approaches have attempted to predict circuit reliability, they often suffer from topological blindness and operate as uninterpretable "black boxes."In this study, we propose an Integrated Machine Learning and Explainable AI (XAI) framework for pre-execution quantum circuit analysis.Using the QUASAR Quantum Reliability Dataset v1 (50,000 synthetic circuits), we evaluate tree-based ensemble models for both continuous reliability regression and categorical classification.Our results demonstrate that HistGradientBoosting achieves superior predictive performance (R 2  0.945 for regression; 88.86% accuracy for classification) under rigorous grouped cross-validation.Furthermore, unsupervised clustering reveals four distinct "reliability archetypes," proving that circuit reliability is driven by a multidimensional interplay of qubit count, depth, and gate composition rather than a single metric.Post-hoc explainability techniques (SHAP, Permutation Importance, and Partial Dependence Plots) identify qubit count, circuit depth, and measurement-related features as primary drivers of reliability degradation.Finally, we critically examine the methodological caveats of synthetic data, target determinism, and feature multicollinearity, establishing a foundational baseline for interpretable quantum software engineering while highlighting the necessity for future hardware-level validation.

title: 17th Conference on Data Analysis Methods for Software Systems
authors: Jolita Bernatavičienė
abstract: This book contains the abstracts of the presentations delivered at the 17th Conference on Data Analysis Methods for Software Systems (DAMSS 2026). The conference takes place on 26–28 November 2026 at the Europa Royale Hotel in Druskininkai, Lithuania.Over seventeen editions, DAMSS has become the place where Lithuanian researchers and developers working in informatics, data analysis, and complex software systems meet every year. Most participants come from universities and research institutes, and they are joined by industry professionals working on practical problems. The conference brings together people with very different experience. Some develop new methods, others apply them in real systems, and others work on problems for which suitable methods do not yet exist. This community grows every year. This year, 135 participants registered for the conference and 95 presentations are included in the programme, both more than last year. Participants come from nine countries: Czechia, Greece, Lithuania, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland, Taiwan, and the United Kingdom. The conference creates new opportunities for future partnership.Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how software systems are built, how data are analysed and how research is carried out. These changes are happening faster than they can be evaluated or settled into established practice. For this reason, one of the most important goals of DAMSS today is the open sharing of experience. Participants discuss what works and what has not worked, the challenges that arise when implementing AI solutions, and the questions that remain unanswered. Such experience is rarely reflected in publications, but it is precisely this kind of experience that enables colleagues to streamline their work and identify the best solutions more quickly.

title: Benchmarking quantum feature encoding strategies for binary classification with QSVM
authors: Murat Kurt
journal: Frontiers in Quantum Science and Technology
abstract: Quantum feature maps determine the mapping of classical data into quantum states and the similarity structure induced by quantum kernels. This study investigates the effects of incorporating statistical relationships between features into quantum encoding on classification performance and circuit resources. Five quantum feature maps based on Pearson correlation, Spearman correlation, Kendall correlation, mutual information, and distance correlation were compared with Angle-RY, H + RY, Z, and ZZ maps with three different connectivity topologies. Classical SVM results with an RBF kernel were also computed for comparison. Experiments were conducted on 500 samples selected from each of five binary classification datasets. Performance was evaluated using class-wise metrics, macro and weighted averages, ROC-AUC, log-loss, and confidence intervals; Holm correction was applied to paired comparisons. The findings showed that no feature map consistently outperformed the others across all tasks and metrics. The numerical gains achieved by dependency-based maps on some tasks did not translate into an overall statistically significant advantage over Angle-RY or classical SVM. Quantum Encoding Feature Score (QFES) scores, defined independently of execution times and combining macro F1 and AUC with the training–test gap and decomposed circuit resources, were computed. The results indicate that quantum feature maps should be selected by jointly considering predictive performance, class balance, uncertainty, and circuit resources.

title: Emulating non-Markovian system-bath dynamics with parametrically driven cavities
authors: Valentin Boettcher, Félix Pellerin, Philippe St-Jean, W. A. Coish
abstract: We introduce and characterize a scheme for emulating non-Markovian quantum system-bath dynamics using the discrete electromagnetic field modes of a parametrically driven cavity. In this scheme, the character of a bosonic bath (the form of the bath spectral density) is tied directly to the shape of the real-time waveform describing periodic parametric cavity modulation. As an explicit example, we demonstrate the feasibility of this scheme for a fiber-loop experiment with currently achievable parameters, supported by numerical simulations and analytical estimates. In particular, we show that a localization transition of the spin-boson model can be accurately emulated in this fiber-loop cavity system. This localization effect is characterized by a sharp transition from partial decay to complete decay for a two-level system coupled to a bosonic bath as the bath spectral density J ( ω ) ∝ ω s is continously tuned from the sub-ohmic ( s < 1 ) to the super-ohmic ( s > 1 ) regime. The transition is only exactly realized in the thermodynamic limit (for an infinite number of bath modes) and for sufficiently weak system-bath coupling. We highlight a competition between the weak-coupling and thermodynamic limits in this problem and show that challenges in approximately realizing the transition can nevertheless be overcome. Finally, we provide bounds on the systematic error introduced when emulating non-Markovian dynamics for arbitrary system observables. The scheme presented here can enable the realization of a modular platform for engineering custom non-Markovian baths, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics, thermalization of many-body systems, and resource-efficient quantum simulations of open quantum systems.

title: Automated construction and verification of unextendible product bases
authors: Zicheng Han, Wanchen Zhang, Fei Shi, Xiande Zhang
journal: Journal of Physics A Mathematical and Theoretical
abstract: Unextendible product bases (UPBs) are important structures in quantum information theory, with applications to completely entangled subspaces, bound entanglement, and local indistinguishability. Since many properties and applications of UPBs are closely related to their sizes, one of the central problems in the study of UPBs is to determine whether UPBs of prescribed sizes exist in a given multipartite system. In this paper, we introduce a SAT-assisted framework based on decompositions of the N-dimensional hypercube. We define O_N-tile decompositions and prove a tile-to-UPB theorem: every O_N-tile decomposition induces a UPB through a construction based on tile-wise Fourier product bases and a global stopper state. We then encode the search for such decompositions as a Boolean satisfiability (SAT) problem and use SAT solvers to generate explicit instances. In terms of verification, we also implement a UPB verification algorithm based on local orthogonality graphs and unsaturated subspaces. The algorithm can be used to determine whether an arbitrary finite set of product states forms a UPB. Using this framework, we obtain UPBs of several sizes in some tripartite and quadripartite systems, including sizes 7, 11, 12, ..., 23 in C^3 ⊗ C^3 ⊗ C^3. Moreover, the small-dimensional instances obtained here can serve as seed UPBs for recursive constructions, leading to further examples in larger multipartite systems.

title: Fast pulses for high-fidelity circularization of interacting Rydberg atoms
authors: Matthias Hüls, Aurore-Alice Young, C. Sayrin, M. Brune, J. M. Raimond, Tommaso Calarco, Felix Motzoi, Robert Zeier
abstract: Circular states in Rydberg atoms offer a promising platform for quantum computation, quantum simulation and quantum sensing. However, the final step of their preparation - termed as circularization, a process that involves the transfer of a large amount of angular momentum quanta to the valence electron by means of radio-frequency (RF) pulses - remains as a major bottleneck for all technological applications based on interacting circular Rydberg atoms. Even though successfully implemented to circularize an atom cloud in the dilute regime, previous efforts to speed up the circularization process have focused on the single-atom case, thereby neglecting the interactions which constitute one of the main resources for quantum simulation and computation. In this theoretical work we show how interactions between two atoms disturb the efficiency of pulses designed for single atoms and identify shifts induced by the interactions on relevant transition energies as the dominant disturbance. We demonstrate that the initial efficiency of single-atom pulses can be restored by adapting them to these shifts. Our approach is based on a simple functional form depending only on two linear parameters determined by the pair arrangement, which we derive analytically. The adapted pulses prepare two ⁸⁷Rb atoms after 65 ns in a n = 52 circular state with a fidelity of at least least 95 % for interatomic distances down to 6.3 μm and for all angular configurations, while also complying experimental amplitude and frequency constraints. Finally, we show that when combining our adapted pulses with Krotov's pulse-shaping algorithm we obtain high-fidelity pulses for any pair arrangement with interatomic distances larger than 5.9 μm. This work demonstrates that fast RF pulses can circularize interacting Rydberg atoms, paving the way toward their technological application.

title: Long-range nonstabilizerness of topologically encoded states from mutual information
authors: David Aram Korbany, Tyler D. Ellison, David T. Stephen, Lorenzo Piroli
abstract: We study long-range nonstabilizerness (LRN), namely the obstruction to remove nonstabilizerness with shallow-depth local quantum circuits. In one-dimensional settings, the mutual information between disconnected spatial regions has proven to be a powerful tool to diagnose LRN. In this work, we focus on encoded states of two-dimensional topologically-ordered systems, and explore the ability of the mutual information to serve as a diagnostic of LRN. Focusing on the concrete setting of lattice models defined on a torus, we show that information about LRN can be gained from the analysis of the mutual information between non-overlapping regions containing non-contractible loops, and of the change of such mutual information under modular real-space transformations. We exemplify this idea in the toric code and the non-abelian string-net model with doubled Fibonacci topological order. In the former case, we show that the mutual information provides a full classification, certifying LRN for all encoded non-stabilizer states. In the latter case, instead, our approach does not lead to a full classification, as it detects LRN for all states except from a finite subset with special transformation properties under the modular group. Finally, we discuss how our results on LRN constrain the logical gates that can be implemented fault-tolerantly on the torus.

title: Optical quantum teleportation with known amplitude distorting factors of teleported qubits
authors: Mikhail S. Podoshvedov, Sergey A. Podoshvedov
abstract: We develop a quantum teleportation protocol of an unknown optical single-rail qubit using a hybrid quantum channel consisting of continuous variable (CV) states of certain parity and photonic states. The quantum channel is characterized by two parameters: a squeezing parameter of single-mode squeezed vacuum (SMSV) state and the beam splitter (BS) parameter, which can be appropriately tuned to improve the protocol efficiency. The CV part of the hybrid state interacts with the single-rail qubit on balanced BS at Alice's location, while discrete variable (DV) half of the quantum channel is controlled by Bob. In half the cases, Bob receives the original qubit, and in almost half the remaining cases, he obtains the input qubit with distorted amplitudes, with both participants knowing the values of the distortion coefficients. As the amount of classical information transmitted by Alice increases, they both gain greater access to partial information about the unitary transformations undergone by the teleported qubits, allowing Bob to continue using them or attempt to recover them to improve the efficiency of the protocol. The proposed probabilistic method for restoring the original qubit from an amplitude distorted one allows increasing the overall probability of the protocol to more than 0.5. The proposed method is a generalization of quantum teleportation, in which a nonlocal photon serves as the quantum channel for transmitting a single-rail qubit.

title: Efficient construction of time-invariant process tensors for simulating high-dimensional non-Markovian open quantum systems
authors: Émile Cochin, Jonathan Keeling, Brendon W. Lovett, Alex W. Chin
abstract: Numerical methods for obtaining exact dynamics of non-Markovian open quantum systems are mostly limited to either small systems or to short-time evolution only. Here, we propose a new algorithm for computing process tensors—matrix product operator (MPO) representations that capture the environment influence—which achieves greatly enhanced computational scalings with system size, while maintaining linear scaling with simulation length. We build on recent developments in the field which allow for long-time evolutions through process tensors which have a time-translational invariance. These can be built for general Gaussian environments and generic coupling operators with the system using infinite time-evolving block decimation (iTEBD). We introduce a modified iTEBD algorithm using intermediate compression steps which bring down the computation time scaling with system size d d from \mathcal{O}(d^8) 𝒪 (d 8) to \mathcal{O}(d^4) 𝒪 (d 4), as well as significantly lowering the required memory. To illustrate the power of this method, we apply it to the problem of dispersive qubit readout in circuit QED, which was previously out-of-reach numerically. The full treatment of the measurement resonator, which requires a large system space, combined with the long simulation times precipitated by the separation of timescales between the measurement drive and the environment dissipation, is now possible. The algorithm we introduce not only allows for capturing non-Markovian dynamics in large open quantum systems, but also further extends all the existing capabilities of process tensors, for example in quantum optimal control, or in computation of multi-time correlations or of steady states, to more complex systems with tens of levels.

title: A Quantum Computing Framework for VLBI Data Correlation
authors: Lei Liu
abstract: This work presents a quantum computing framework for very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) data correlation. It is shown that a classical baseband time series data of a length N can be embedded into a quantum superposition state using amplitude encoding with only log2N qubits. The basic VLBI correlation and fringe fitting operations, including fringe rotation, a Fourier transform, delay compensation, and cross correlation, can be implemented via quantum algorithms with significantly reduced computational complexity. A single-baseline quantum pipeline for geodetic VLBI data processing is constructed, and its feasibility and accuracy are validated through direct comparison with a classical pipeline. Amplitude encoding of large data volumes remains the primary bottleneck in quantum computing. However, the quantized nature of VLBI raw data helps reduce the state preparation complexity. This investigation demonstrates that quantum computation offers a promising paradigm for VLBI data correlation and is likely to play a role in future VLBI systems.

title: Topology aware quantum circuit cutting via reinforcement learning
authors: Abhishek Sadhu, Aritra Sarkar, Akash Kundu
abstract: Simulating molecular systems on quantum processors has the potential to surpass classical methods in computational resource efficiency. The limited qubit connectivity, small processor size, and short coherence times of near-term quantum hardware constrain the applicability of quantum algorithms like quantum phase estimation and variational quantum eigensolver. Quantum circuit cutting has the potential to address these constraints by partitioning large circuits into smaller subcircuits, enabling execution on resource-limited devices. However, standard graph-theoretic partitioning often fails to account for the entanglement structure of the quantum state, leading to partitions that minimize wire cuts at the cost of increasing the simulation error. To address these limitations, in this article, we propose CutQAS, a framework that integrates quantum circuit cutting with quantum architecture search (QAS) to enhance quantum chemistry simulations. Our framework primarily contains two steps. First, an RL agent explores all possible topologies to identify an optimal circuit structure. Subsequently, a second RL agent refines the selected topology by determining optimal circuit cuts, ensuring efficient execution on constrained hardware. We demonstrate that CutQAS implicitly optimizes the Schmidt spectrum truncation, identifying partitions that yield higher accuracy by mapping a 4- and 6-qubit quantum chemistry problem onto a 3-qubit processor. This approach presents an improved solution for quantum chemistry applications, offering a systematic pathway to overcoming hardware constraints in near-term quantum computing.

title: Optimal recoil-free state preparation protocols in an optical atom tweezer
authors: Lia Kley, Nicolas Heimann, Aslam Parvej, Lukas Broers, Ludwig Mathey
abstract: Quantum computing in atom tweezers requires high-fidelity implementations of quantum operations. Here, we demonstrate the optimal implementation of the transition $\ket{\downarrow} \rightarrow \ket{\uparrow}$ of two levels, serving as a qubit, of an atom in a tweezer potential, driven by a single-photon Rabi pulse. The Rabi pulse generates a photon recoil of the atom, due to the Lamb-Dicke coupling between the internal and motional degree of freedom, driving the system out of the logical subspace. This detrimental effect is strongly suppressed in the protocols that we propose. Using pulse engineering, we generate optimal protocols composed of a Rabi pulse protocol and a force protocol, corresponding to dynamically displacing the tweezer. We generate these for a large parameter space, from small to large values of the Rabi frequency, and a range of pulse lengths. We identify three main regimes for the optimal protocols, and discuss their properties. In all of these regimes, we demonstrate infidelity well below the current technological standard, thus mitigating a universal challenge in atom tweezers and other quantum technology platforms.

title: Enhancing the Stationary Optomechanical Entanglement and Cooling of a Rotating Mirror in a Laguerre–Gaussian Optomechanical System via Coherent Feedback
authors: Keru Zhu, Sumei Huang, 邓立 Li Deng, Aixi Chen
abstract: Optomechanical entanglement generation and near‐ground‐state cooling of macroscopic mechanical resonators play important roles in probing fundamental physics and develop new quantum applications. Here, we investigate how a coherent feedback loop affects the stationary optomechanical entanglement and the cooling of a rotating mirror in a Laguerre–Gaussian (LG) optomechanical system. By implementing a coherent feedback loop with a beam splitter and three mirrors outside the cavity, a fraction of the output field is fed back into the optical cavity. In the unresolved‐sideband regime, by adjusting the beam‐splitter reflectivity and the feedback phase, the coherent feedback can significantly enhance the entanglement between the LG cavity field and the rotating mirror due to the feedback‐induced reduction in the effective cavity decay rate, and the optomechanical entanglement is shown to persist for ambient temperatures above 150 K. Furthermore, the coherent feedback can effectively suppress the thermal decoherence effect; even in a 50 K environment, the rotating mirror can be brought close to its quantum ground state by tuning the beam‐splitter reflectivity and the feedback phase to suitable values. Moreover, the effect of optical losses in the feedback loop on entanglement and cooling is discussed. We find that these losses degrade both entanglement and cooling performance.

title: Optical gas thermometry with parts-per-million accuracy
