authors: Jin Wang, Yan Tan, Qi Huang, Jin-Ke Li, Cun-Feng Cheng, An-Wen Liu, Shui-Ming Hu
abstract: Optical gas thermometry provides a quantum-based route for primary thermodynamic temperature measurement. This work reports advances in Doppler broadening thermometry (DBT) and line-intensity ratio thermometry (LRT) achieved by implementing cavity mode dispersion spectroscopy (CMDS). The CMDS technique, which relies solely on frequency measurements of cavity-mode dispersive shifts induced by molecular absorption, effectively circumvents the limitations of traditional absorption spectroscopy, such as detector nonlinearity and long-term intensity drifts. We demonstrate record-setting accuracies, with combined standard uncertainties of approximately 12 ppm for DBT and 7 ppm for LRT, establishing the most precise optical thermometry measurements achieved to date. These results validate DBT and LRT as robust, primary thermometry methods grounded in fundamental molecular physics and open new avenues for quantum metrology and precision spectroscopy.

title: Matrix phase-space representations for quantum symmetries
authors: Alexander S. Dellios, M. D. Reid, P. D. Drummond
abstract: We introduce a general phase-space representation that includes global quantum symmetries in the basis expansion. This method, called matrix phase-space, projects the basis onto a reduced Hilbert space, which can greatly reduce sampling errors of many-body quantum simulations when there is a symmetry, and unifies several previous phase-space methods. The purpose of this paper is to provide detailed proofs of basic theorems and operator identities. We also treat several different types of symmetries, corresponding to parity, number, and momentum conservation laws. To illustrate these methods, we give a detailed derivation of previous applications to the topical problem of validating the outputs of Gaussian boson sampling (GBS) quantum computers (QCs) with photon-number-resolving (PNR) detectors. Exact evaluation of GBS PNR output probabilities has exponential classical complexity. Fortunately, special cases of output GBS grouped probabilities have tractable solutions, providing a way to check the results. Using matrix phase-space with parity symmetry, we observe a reduction of over two orders of magnitude in sampling errors compared with earlier methods in low-loss cases. Additional nonlinear examples are also treated. These include the dynamical evolution of a nonlinear damped one-dimensional lattice and the periodic Bose-Hubbard model. More details will be given elsewhere. As well as direct application to experiments, this scalable first-principles method may be useful for validating other QC calculations on large Hilbert spaces.

title: Adaptive quantum metrology with large dynamic range using short one-axis twists
authors: Tyler G. Thurtell, Akimasa Miyake
abstract: Phase estimation with potentially large phase values, i.e., with large dynamic range, has many applications in quantum metrology, for example to atomic clocks. A recently proposed phase estimation scheme approaches the Heisenberg scaling in this global setting using sequences of increasingly squeezed Gaussian states as probes and adaptively chosen, potentially mid-circuit, measurements. In this work, we first observe that the pattern of increase in the squeezing of the probes is applicable even to states with some non-Gaussian features. We then propose an experimentally feasible version of this phase estimation scheme, based on the alternating application of one-axis twist (OAT) operations and rotations. Our protocols are explicitly described in terms of multiple OAT angles whose durations decrease polynomially with system size and spin-squeezing parameters that decay as N − μ , with μ > 2 / 3 in most cases. Using numerical computation of the system-size dependence N − ν of the Bayesian mean-squared error of an estimator, we show that these states are suitable for use in the phase estimation scheme, and highlight the protocols to achieve ν = 17 / 9 and 53 / 27 using two and three OAT operations respectively in the last adaptation stage. We also analyze the limited non-Gaussianity of the resulting probe states and discuss the role of non-Gaussianity in this protocol more generally. Finally, we analyze how robust these protocols are with respect to imperfections such as particle number fluctuations and coherent control fluctuations.

title: Digital Twin Networks for 6G Wireless Systems: Architecture, Enabling Technologies, AI-Driven Control, and Open Challenges
authors: Charalampos Oikonomidis, Emmanouel T. Michailidis, Demosthenes Vouyioukas, Nikolaos I. Miridakis
abstract: The transition to the Sixth Generation (6G) of mobile networks requires proactive and deterministic orchestration to satisfy the stringent key performance indicators of future services, including ultra-reliable low-latency communications, enhanced mobile broadband, and massive machine-type communications. Digital Twin Networks (DTNs) have emerged as a foundational technology to meet these demands, offering real-time and high-fidelity virtual replicas of the physical network. Although the literature explores DTNs conceptually, a gap exists in the coverage of technical classification and computational feasibility evaluations. This survey addresses this gap by formally categorizing state-of-the-art DTN architectures into passive monitoring twins and active control twins. We evaluate their enabling technologies, namely ray-tracing, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, artificial intelligence, and multi-access edge computing. Importantly, we analyze the complexity of ten state-of-the-art frameworks, five reporting complexity expressions, four derived in this survey, and one not derivable, to assess hardware scalability and inference bottlenecks. These architectures are then linked to forthcoming 6G use cases, including smart cities, Industry 5.0, healthcare, and smart grids. Finally, we synthesize crucial unresolved challenges, highlighting graphics processing unit hardware limitations, cyber-physical actuation latency, and the need for a zero-trust security paradigm, offering research directions toward the unified Internet of Everything.

title: Quantum timekeeping and the dynamics of scrambling in critical systems
authors: Devjyoti Tripathy, Federico Centrone, Sebastian Deffner
abstract: Interacting quantum many-body systems can rapidly scramble quantum information, raising the question of how precisely local subsystems can track the passage of time during this evolution. In this work, we develop a quantum metrological framework for quantum chaos by showing that local subsystems of information scrambling systems naturally function as quantum stopwatches. The reduced quantum state of a subsystem encodes the passage of time through its local temporal distinguishability along its dynamical trajectory. Treating time as the estimation parameter, we then derive a generalized quantum Cramer-Rao bound that directly relates the precision of time estimation to the decay of out-of-time ordered correlators (OTOCs) and subsystem quantum Fisher information (QFI). For a single qubit subsystem, we obtain an exact relation between the incoherent component of subsystem QFI and the decay rate of OTOCs in quantumly chaotic dynamics, while the total subsystem QFI provides an upper bound to the corresponding decay rate. Furthermore, using a scaling analysis based on imaginary-time correlators, we investigate under what conditions the incoherent subsystem QFI exhibits critical amplification near quantum phase transitions. Our results are demonstrated and verified by a numerical analysis of the dynamics of a chaotic Ising chain.

title: Superposed quantum evolutions across chaotic and regular regimes
authors: Amit Kumar Anand, Anne-Catherine de la Hamette, Robert B. Mann, Shohini Ghose
abstract: While the superposition of quantum evolutions is known to produce interference effects, the interference between evolutions with regular and chaotic classical limits remains largely unexplored. Here, we use a Mach-Zehnder interferometer to investigate the superposition of two quantum evolutions, implemented via postselection, and to compare it with the corresponding classical mixture. The quantum kicked top provides a natural platform for this study, as its classical dynamics ranges from regular to mixed to fully chaotic depending on the Hamiltonian parameters. We show that when a regular evolution is superposed with a chaotic one, the resulting subsystem entropy can exceed that of the classical mixture, provided the contribution of the chaotic branch dominates in the superposed quantum evolution. We further demonstrate that entropy production in such superpositions is strongly influenced by the structure of the underlying classical phase space. We further show that increased entropy generation can occur for purely regular dynamics at small values of the chaos parameter, given an appropriate choice of postselection. These results reveal a nontrivial interplay between classical chaos and quantum interference in superposed quantum dynamics.

title: Resolving topological obstructions to vectorial structured field control
authors: An Aloysius Wang, Yuxi Cai, Yifei Ma, Patrick S. Salter, Chao He
abstract: The use of structured matter, such as optical retarders, for vectorial control is a well-established and widely used technique in modern optics, and has driven continued advances in the manipulation of complex, spatially varying vectorial fields. However, achieving arbitrary field conversion typically requires the use of cascaded elements, as intrinsic physical and fabrication constraints fundamentally limit individual devices to a restricted subset of transformations. This results in an overall continuous transformation potentially failing to be continuous at the level of the parameters of the cascade, leading to detrimental engineering consequences such as the introduction of complex, discontinuous aberrations that disrupt important topological properties of the underlying light and matter fields. In this work, we establish a mathematical framework for analyzing the topological difficulties that emerge in the decomposition of an overall transformation into individual layers, and for determining the minimal depth required to overcome them. The strategy introduced provides a general pathway for optimizing designs for vectorial field control and matter field generation, with particular importance for the manipulation of topological phases in optical polarization fields, such as Stokes skyrmions, where continuity is of vital importance.

title: Reconstructing the unitary part of a noisy quantum channel
authors: Adrian Romer, Daniel M. Reich, Christiane P. Koch
abstract: We consider the problem of reconstructing, from a set of input and output states, the unitary describing the evolution of a quantum system or quantum channel. For ideal, fully coherent evolution, we show that the unitary can be reconstructed from two mixed states or d + 1 pure states, where d is the size of Hilbert space. The reconstruction method can be extended to approximate the unitary part of a dynamical map, provided the decoherence is not too strong to render this question meaningless. We exemplify the method for the example of the cross-resonance gate as well as a random set of unitaries, comparing the reconstruction from pure, respectively mixed, states to an approach based on the Choi matrix. We find that the pure state reconstruction requires the least amount of resources when the dynamics is close to unitary, whereas the mixed state approach outperforms the pure state reconstruction in terms of channel uses for appreciable decoherence. These conclusions hold also in the presence of state preparation and measurement errors and irrespective of the Hilbert space size.

title: High-resolution image-projection fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy
authors: Woong Jae Baek, Jongchan Park, Liang S. Gao
abstract: Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) provides molecular contrast that is largely independent of fluorophore concentration, yet it remains constrained by a persistent trade-off among acquisition speed, photon dose, and detector complexity. To address this challenge, we developed image-projection fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (IP-FLIM), an integrated optical and computational platform that enables high-resolution, component-resolved lifetime imaging using only a linear single-photon avalanche diode array. We validate IP-FLIM using fluorescent microbeads and bovine pulmonary artery endothelial cells, demonstrating up to 22.3× improvement in contrast-to-noise ratio and 72.3% reduction in background noise over conventional filtered back-projection reconstruction. By combining wide-field projection acquisition with computational k -space reconstruction, IP-FLIM provides a scalable route to fast, high-resolution multiplex lifetime imaging.

title: Co-optimization of Spin Coherence and Valley Splitting in Si/SiGe Heterostructures
authors: Peihong Zhang, Xuedong Hu, Saif Ullah, J. R. Petta
abstract: Single electron spins can be used to encode and process information in semiconductor quantum devices. Progress has been hindered by materials challenges, such as the small energy splitting between low-lying valley states and hyperfine coupling to nuclear spins. Here we use density functional theory to optimize the valley splitting and spin dephasing time in realistic Si/SiGe heterostructures. Reductions in the Si quantum well width generally increase the valley splitting. However, in narrow quantum wells, a larger fraction of the electronic wavefunction resides in the SiGe buffer layers, which increases the hyperfine coupling with spinful [73]Ge. Our work shows that Si/SiGe heterostructures with 3 – 4 nm wide quantum wells and [73]Ge and [29]Si concentrations of 50 ppm should support average valley splittings Ev > 500 µeV and spin dephasing times T2[∗] [exceeding 15][ µ][s] assuming an effective quantum dot area of 700 nm[2]. In addition, sharper Si/SiGe interfaces in general result in larger valley splittings and longer spin dephasing times.

title: Logarithmic-depth quantum state preparation of polynomials
authors: Baptiste Claudon, Alexis Lucas, Jean-Philip Piquemal, César Feniou, Julien Zylberman
abstract: Quantum state preparation is a central primitive in many quantum algorithms, yet it is generally resource intensive, with efficient constructions known only for structured families of states. This work introduces a method for preparing quantum states whose amplitudes are given by a degree − d polynomial, using circuits with logarithmic depth in the number n of qubits and only O (n) ancilla qubits, improving previous approaches that required linear-depth circuits. The construction first relies on a block-encoding of an affine diagonal operator based on its Pauli-basis decomposition, which involves only n terms. A modified linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) technique is introduced to implement this decomposition in logarithmic depth, together with a novel circuit for the EXACT-one oracle that flags basis states in which exactly one qubit is in the state | 1 ⟩. It then uses a generalized quantum eigenvalue transformation (GQET) to promote this affine operator to an arbitrary degree polynomial. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations are reported along with a proof-of-principle implementation on a Quantinuum System Model H2 trapped-ion quantum processor using 14 qubits and more than 500 primitive quantum gates. Because polynomial approximations are ubiquitous in scientific computing, this construction provides a scalable and resource-efficient approach to quantum state preparation, further improving the potential of quantum algorithms in fields such as chemistry, physics, engineering, and finance.

title: Atomic interface for high-dimensional temporal mode quantum networks
authors: Shicheng Zhang, Aonan Zhang, Ilse Maillette de Buy Wenniger, Paul Burdekin, Jerzy Szuniewicz, Steven Sagona-Stophel, Sarah E. Thomas, Ian A. Walmsley
abstract: Photonic temporal modes are an attractive encoding basis for high-dimensional quantum networks due to their high channel capacity and fiber compatibility. However, realizing their full potential requires devices capable of synchronizing, processing and interfacing these modes across photonic and atomic bandwidths. Here, we demonstrate a programmable high-dimensional temporal mode processor based on a Raman quantum memory in warm cesium vapor. Exploiting the single-mode nature of the Raman interaction kernel, we dynamically shape the control field to synthesize a tunable coherent filter that selectively addresses user-defined temporal waveforms. Operating with 50 ns pulses, we characterize the mode-selectivity of the filter across 30 orthogonal Hermite-Gaussian modes, with five-dimensional process tomography yielding an efficiency-normalized filtering fidelity of 0.955(7). Independent shaping of the read control field further enables programmable temporal-mode conversion with uniform efficiencies comparable to those of mode-preserving storage and retrieval. Moreover, we demonstrate tenfold bandwidth compression and expansion of 10~ns pulses, offering a coherent interface between GHz- and MHz-bandwidth network nodes. These results establish the potential of Raman quantum memories as active nodes for scalable quantum information processing.

title: Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing
authors: Ziyue Hua, Chuanlong Ma, Yilong Zhou, Yifang Xu, Zi-Jie Chen, Weizhou Cai, Jiajun Chen, Lintao Xiao

title: Coherent manipulation of interacting electron qubits on solid neon
authors: Xinhao Li, Yizhong Huang, Xu Han, Xianjing Zhou, Amir Yacoby, Dafei Jin
abstract: Electrons trapped on solid neon surfaces serve as low-noise charge qubits with long coherence times and high operational fidelities. Such charge qubits offer full electrical control and compact device footprints, convenient for scaling up with quantum circuits. Realizing two-qubit gates on this platform is a critical step towards practical quantum information processing. In this work, we report the first experimental demonstration of coherent manipulation of multiple interacting electron-on-solid-neon (eNe) charge qubits. By exploiting the electrons naturally confined in close proximity by the surface structures of solid neon, we have achieved a direct qubit-qubit coupling strength of up to 62.5 MHz, as well as implemented cross-resonance (CR) and bSWAP two-qubit gates using global microwave drives. The natural electron confinement by solid neon mitigates the high-density-wiring challenge, simplifies the multi-qubit control, and establishes a unique path to scale up the eNe qubit platform.

title: Optimal Calibration of Qubit Detuning and Crosstalk
authors: David Shnaiderov, Matan Ben Dov, Yoav Woldiger, Assaf Hamo, Eugene Demler, Emanuele G. Dalla Torre
abstract: Characterizing and calibrating physical qubits is essential for maintaining the performance of quantum processors. A key challenge in this process is crosstalk, which complicates the estimation of individual qubit detunings. In this work, we derive optimal strategies for estimating detuning and crosstalk parameters by optimizing Ramsey interference experiments using Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound. We compare several calibration protocols, including measurements of a single quadrature at multiple times and of two quadratures at a single time, for a fixed number of total measurements. Our results predict that the latter approach yields the highest precision and robustness in both cases of isolated and coupled qubits. We validate our approach experimentally using both a single NV center and superconducting transmon qubits. Our approach enables accurate parameter extraction with significantly fewer measurements, resulting in up to a 50% reduction in calibration time while maintaining estimation accuracy.

title: Machine learning models in FinTech for sustainable innovation: a comprehensive empirical evaluation with the S.A.F.E. framework
authors: Girish Paliwal, Pragya Paliwal
abstract: Recent FinTech credit and risk systems demonstrate a marked tendency to utilize machine learning methodologies; still, conventional evaluation benchmarks focus almost exclusively on predictive accuracy. This narrow focus gives rise to a challenging problem. The present study focuses on the fact that the AI Act and the Fair Credit Reporting Act penalize operational carbon footprints, systemic demographic bias and opaque decision logic. In order to address this evident gap in the literature, an evaluation of algorithmic trade-offs is conducted using the four-pillar S.A.F.E. framework (Sustainability, Accuracy, Fairness, Explainability) across three operational domains. The following subjects will be explored the detection of credit fraud; the corporate ESG rating; and geospatial physical climate risk. We benchmark five diverse architectures an Explainable Stacking Ensemble, Enhanced Random Forest, XGBoost, a Feedforward Neural Network, and a simulated Quantum SVM across 160,000 synthetic records calibrated to Lending Club, MSCI ESG, and NOAA distributions. Nonparametric Friedman tests confirm significant performance divergence among the models (chi-square = 18.24, df = 4, p = 0.0011). Although Enhanced Random Forest achieves peak raw accuracy in fraud screening (97.90% ± 0.40%), the Explainable Stacking Ensemble secures the highest composite S.A.F.E. score (9.28/10, Grade A+ ), pairing an F1-score of 0.972 with high TreeSHAP explanation fidelity (0.941). Conversely, the simulated QSVM exhibits a substantial classical latency penalty (145.0 ms/pred). Multi-attribute sensitivity tests across four contrasting stakeholder regimes demonstrate that ensemble superiority remains strictly invariant to policy weighting (W = 1.00). These findings provide risk managers and regulators with an empirical roadmap for the deployment of high-performing models that satisfy statutory fairness and environmental mandates.

title: Performance evaluation of a photon-based quantum router network for Kathmandu Metropolitan City
authors: Chitran Pokhrel, Babu Ram Dawadi, Bishnu Prasad Gautam
abstract: Deploying quantum communication networks in dense cities is challenging because photon loss, noise, and inefficient entanglement distribution degrade fidelity and increase latency. Conventional repeater chains add intermediate nodes along each fiber span, and housing quantum memories at such mid-span sites in a dense city is operationally demanding. This study evaluates a photon-based quantum router network for Kathmandu Metropolitan City in which entanglement buffering and swapping are performed only at quantum router (RTR) nodes co-located with existing network sites. On an infrastructure-derived topology of 12 routers and 14 fiber links, the simulated network achieves a mean fidelity of 0.925 (95% CI 0.916–0.934), a mean throughput of 1159.5 ebps, and a mean latency of 15.28 ms over 83 completed requests. A closed-form multi-hop model, consistent with the simulation for single links, shows that end-to-end fidelity is limited mainly by hop count and by memory and detector efficiency rather than by urban fiber loss, that mid-span repeaters lower the rate on spans shorter than about 9 km, and that the router-only design remains viable for spans up to about 50 km. A simulation of the Illinois Express Quantum Network topology gives fidelity and latency of the same order as reported experimentally.

title: Quantum Algorithms for Computational Fluid Dynamics
authors: Mario Guillaume Cecile, Nis-Luca van Hülst, Tomohiro Hashizume, Pia Siegl, Anonymous, José Diogo Da Costa Jesus, Paul Over, Sergio Bengoechea
abstract: We present a comprehensive review of quantum approaches for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) arising in computational fluid dynamics (CFD). We examine fully quantum approaches, including quantum linear system algorithms (QLSAs), ranging from the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd (HHL) algorithm to quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), Hamiltonian simulation, and quantum lattice Boltzmann methods (QLBMs), while emphasizing hybrid quantum–classical approaches, including quantum-physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) and amplitude-encoded variational PDE solvers. We focus on hardware-agnostic algorithms compatible with present noisy processors and emerging fault-tolerant architectures. For each framework, we analyze the mathematical formulation, algorithmic structure, and principal limitations. We also examine tensor-network (TN) representations, since CFD fields, differential operators, and geometrical information can often be encoded efficiently in low-rank form. The TN formalism bridges CFD discretizations and quantum states, operators, and circuits, enabling compact representations to be translated into tensor-programmable variational quantum algorithms (TP-VQAs). We further review benchmark problems, including Poisson, reaction, diffusion, and nonlinear model equations, and assess how well quantum algorithms capture key features of fluid dynamics. Our analysis highlights that potential quantum advantage is highly problem dependent and governed by condition number, representational complexity, state preparation, and measurement constraints. We outline capabilities, limitations, and challenges toward scalable quantum algorithms for CFD.

title: Non-Gaussianity in cat codes: global incompatibility and local geometric alignment with the magic resource
authors: Yuwei Zhu, Seungbeom Chin, William J. Munro, Kae Nemoto
abstract: Non-Gaussianity is an essential resource for genuine quantum advantages in continuous-variable quantum systems and is regarded as a counterpart of the magic resource in discrete-variable systems. Recently, an exact correspondence between non-Gaussianity (NG) and the magic resource was identified within the Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) encoding framework. Whether such a relation persists beyond GKP encoding, however, remains unclear. Here, we address this question in the cat-code setting. By comparing the Wigner logarithmic negativity (WLN) and a magic measure defined from a phase-operator basis, we analyze the resource geometry of non-degenerate $d$-peaked cat states. We find that cat codes do not inherit the global value-preserving GKP magic--NG equivalence, but their asymptotic WLN geometry allows a constructive local alignment with the magic-measure geometry. Specifically, the sector-adapted asymptotic cat construction has the same local phase-rotation invariance as the magic measure for general $d$, while the qubit construction establishes an explicit local alignment of their complete level-set contours. We also examine how thermal attenuation changes the finite-code contour geometry and the surviving WLN contrast. These results identify both the global incompatibility and the locally constructive relation between magic and non-Gaussian resources in cat codes, suggesting a geometry-based approach to resource correspondences beyond the GKP framework.

title: Logical entangling by qubit permutations in hypergraph products
authors: Keming He, Ziao Tang, Zetong Li, Ge Bai, Xin Eric Wang
abstract: Logical entangling gates are a major source of physical spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Phantom codes reduce this cost by implementing every ordered in-block logical CNOT through physical qubit permutations and Pauli-frame updates. Whether this mechanism can coexist with qLDPC structure is a central question for low-overhead fault-tolerant architectures. We give a complete answer within binary CSS hypergraph product (HGP) codes. Up to natural equivalences, phantomness singles out the simplex–repetition family. The same symmetry further extends to the full in-block logical Clifford group. We evaluate this family under circuit-level noise in logical GHZ-state preparation and Trotterized many-body quantum simulation. With ideally prepared Steane ancillas, the HGP code yields lower observable mismatch rates than the rotated surface-code baseline at distance eight. Reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays offer a natural setting for this approach, supporting nonlocal qLDPC operations while enabling in-block logical CNOTs without additional physical operations. Together, these results connect code symmetry, logical-gate overhead, and qLDPC design, and motivate phantom families with improved asymptotic parameters.

title: Coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains
authors: Francesco Zatelli, Bart Roovers, Nick van Loo, Antonio Lombardi, Juan D. Torres Luna, Sebastian Miles, Vincent P. M. Sietses, Florian J. Bennebroek Evertsz’

title: Quantum-Accelerated Self-Consistent Field: A Hybrid Algorithm
authors: Alexis Ralli, Tim Weaving, Thomas M. Bickley, Peter V. Coveney, Peter J. Love
journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
abstract: We present the Grover adaptive search self-consistent field (GAS-SCF) algorithm. GAS-SCF leverages quantum arithmetic to construct an efficient oracle that marks target states (Fock states) which improve upon some initial classical energy estimate. Amplitude amplification then increases the probability of measuring these states. This approach offers a theoretical quadratic speed-up for the optimization problem encountered in SCF quantum chemistry and establishes a baseline against which structured optimization algorithms, such as QAOA and DQI, may be compared. In this work, we classically simulate three examples as proofs of concept of the algorithm, the largest consisting of 26 qubits. We then extend our analysis to two larger systems, with O3 representing the largest case at 330 qubits. These examples are chosen to probe classically challenging SCF regimes. Achieving chemically relevant applications of GAS-SCF will require large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: Quantum in biology, quantum for biology, and biology for quantum: mapping the evidence and the road ahead
authors: Lea Gassab, Betony Adams, Yashine H. Goolam Hossen, Abbas Hassasfar, Onur Pusuluk, Nirosha J. Murugan, Iannis K. Kominis, Özgür Esat Müstecaplıoğlu
abstract: Quantum science and biology now intersect in three complementary directions: quantum in biology, quantum for biology, and biology for quantum. This review provides a structured narrative evidence map of that interface rather than an exhaustive catalogue or formal systematic review. For each topic, we ask what the mechanistic or technological claim is, which quantum resource is invoked, what the strongest experiments and models establish, which classical alternatives or engineering confounds remain competitive, and which tests or benchmarks would most strongly change confidence. A compact mathematical framework relates Hamiltonian couplings, environmental decoherence, barrier penetration, spin-dependent reaction yields, and matched perturbations to biological observables. The most mature quantum-in-biology cases remain mechanistically constrained tunneling in some enzymatic hydrogen-transfer reactions and radical-pair spin chemistry as a viable framework for magnetoreception, whereas several higher-visibility topics remain suggestive but unresolved under physiological conditions. In quantum for biology, the central issue is whether quantum-enabled tools improve biological inference relative to strong classical baselines under realistic calibration, dose, throughput, and uncertainty constraints. In biology for quantum, the strongest claims arise when biomolecular structure or self-assembly measurably improves fabrication, integration, or robustness in quantum devices. Summary tables in the Appendix provide a compact cross-map view of the current evidence, major confounds, and the experiments or benchmarks most likely to discriminate between competing explanations.

title: Minimum weight decoding in the colour code is NP-hard
authors: Mark Walters, Mark L. Turner
abstract: All utility-scale quantum computers will require some form of Quantum Error Correction in which logical qubits are encoded in a larger number of physical qubits. One promising encoding is known as the colour code which has broad applicability across all qubit types and can decisively reduce the overhead of certain logical operations when compared to other two-dimensional topological codes such as the surface code. However, whereas the surface code decoding problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time by finding minimum weight matchings in a graph, prior to this work, it was not known whether exact and efficient colour code decoding was possible. Optimism in this area, stemming from the colour code’s significant structure and well understood similarities to the surface code, fanned this uncertainty. In this paper we resolve this, proving that exact decoding of the colour code is NP-hard – that is, there does not exist a polynomial time algorithm unless P=NP. This highlights a notable contrast to some of the colour code’s key competitors, such as the surface code, and motivates continued work in the narrower space of heuristic and approximate algorithms for fast, accurate and scalable colour code decoding.

title: Recursive Clifford noise reduction
authors: Aharon Brodutch, Gregory Baimetov, Edwin Tham, Nicolas Delfosse
abstract: Clifford noise reduction CliNR is a partial error correction scheme that reduces the logical error rate of Clifford circuits at the cost of a modest qubit and gate overhead. The CliNR implementation of an n -qubit Clifford circuit of size s achieves a vanishing logical error rate if s n p 2 → 0 where p is the physical error rate. Here, we propose a recursive version of CliNR that can reduce errors on larger circuits with a relatively small gate overhead. When n p → 0, the logical error rate can be vanishingly small. When s p > 2 this can be achieved with (2 ⌈ log ⁡ (s p) ⌉ + 1) n + 1 qubits and at most 24 s ⌈ (s p) 3.6 ⌉ gates. For s p ≤ 2 we recover the original CliNR. Using numerical simulations, we show that the recursive method can offer an advantage in a realistic near-term parameter regime. When circuit sizes are large enough, recursive CliNR can reach a lower logical error rate than the original CliNR with the same gate overhead. The results offer promise for reducing logical errors in large Clifford circuits with relatively small overheads.

title: Directional codes for quantum LDPC error correction on square and hexagonal grid architectures
authors: György Pál Gehér, David Byfield, Archibald Ruban
abstract: Utility-scale quantum computing requires quantum error correction to protect quantum information against noise. Superconducting hardware is a promising platform for fault-tolerant computation, but its typically two-dimensional nearest-neighbour connectivity restricts the variety of quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes that can be implemented efficiently. Here we introduce directional codes, a family of qLDPC codes compatible with square-grid and, in some cases, hexagonal-grid architectures. The key idea is to use the iSWAP gate to measure long range stabilisers using only local interactions, without requiring additional connectivity. We evaluate directional codes using a superconducting-inspired circuit-level Pauli noise model and compare them to the rotated toric code and bivariate bicycle codes. The best directional code family considered matches the logical error rate of the rotated toric code at physical error rate p = 10 −3 but requires only a quarter to a third of the number of physical qubits to encode a given number of logical qubits.

title: Designing fault-tolerant blind quantum computation
authors: Gefen Baranes, Iria W. Wang, Francisco Machado, Aziza Suleymanzade, Pieter-Jan Stas, Yan-Cheng Wei, Susanne F. Yelin, Johannes Borregaard
abstract: Blind quantum computing (BQC) allows a client with limited quantum capabilities to delegate quantum computations to a more powerful server while hiding the computation. Existing protocols face significant challenges when scaling to large-scale fault-tolerant computations due to large communication overhead, photon losses, and low efficiencies. We use a recently demonstrated hybrid light-matter approach [PRL 132, 150604 (2024); Science 388, 509-513 (2025)] to develop a scalable architecture for blind quantum computation. By combining high-fidelity local gates on the server’s matter qubits with delegated rotations using photons, we construct loss-tolerant blind gates that enable new algorithmic design possibilities. Using these tools, the client can compile the algorithm to meet specific privacy goals while using fewer communication resources. We then present a scalable approach for fault-tolerant blind logical algorithms that improves the error-correction threshold and increases the speed and depth of blind logical circuits. Finally, we outline how this architecture can be implemented on state-of-the-art quantum hardware, including neutral atom arrays and solid-state spin defects. These new capabilities open up opportunities for deep circuit blind quantum computing.

title: Sequential decoding of the XYZ 2 hexagonal stabilizer code
authors: Basudha Srivastava, Yinzi Xiao, Anton Frisk Kockum, Ben Criger, Mats Granath
abstract: Quantum error correction requires accurate and efficient decoding to optimally suppress errors in the encoded information. For concatenated codes, where one code is embedded within another, optimal decoding can be achieved using a message-passing algorithm that sends conditional error probabilities from the lower-level code to a higher-level decoder. In this work, we study the XYZ 2 topological stabilizer code, defined on a honeycomb lattice, and use the fact that it can be viewed as a concatenation of a 2, 1, 1 phase-flip parity check code and the surface code with Y Z Z Y stabilizers, to decode the syndrome information in two steps. We use this sequential decoding scheme to correct errors on data qubits, as well as measurement errors, under various biased error models using both a maximum-likelihood decoder (MLD) and more efficient matching-based decoders. For depolarizing noise we find that the sequential matching decoder gives a threshold of 18.3 %, close to optimal, as a consequence of a favorable, effectively biased, error model on the upper-level YZZY code. For phase-biased noise on data qubits, at a bias η = p z p x + p y = 10, we find that a belief-matching-based decoder reaches thresholds of 24.1 %, compared to 28.6 % for the MLD. With measurement errors the thresholds are reduced to 3.4 % and 4.3 %, for depolarizing and biased noise, respectively, using the belief-matching decoder. This demonstrates that the XYZ 2 code has thresholds that are competitive with other codes tailored to biased noise. The results also showcase two essential components in optimizing the performance of concatenated codes: (1) tailoring the upper-level code to the effective noise profile of the decoded lower-level code, and (2) using an upper-level decoder that is adapted to this noise profile.

title: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed-Solomon Codes
authors: Valentina Astore, Martino Borello, Alain Couvreur
abstract: Linearized Reed-Solomon codes (LRS) are optimal sum-rank-metric codes that generalize both Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes, and benefit from excellent decoding capabilities, making them potentially interesting candidates for post-quantum code-based cryptography. Previous works have investigated the underlying geometric structure of LRS codes, identifying geometric invariants that distinguish them from random codes. Other works have proposed approaches to recovering the LRS structure from an arbitrary generator matrix, together with additional data. However, both the distinguishers and the recovery techniques proposed so far are either not fully general, or have a prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a polynomial-time procedure for the full structure recovery of LRS codes from the sole knowledge of an arbitrary generator matrix. Our results show that, like their Hamming and rank metric counterparts, LRS codes cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. Our approach combines Overbeck-type attacks with suitable matrix manipulations and shortening techniques to recover the evaluation parameters across different ranges of code dimensions.

title: Monotonic probes of asymmetry and robustness of the quantum Mpemba effect
authors: Riccardo Travaglino, Michele Mazzoni, Pasquale Calabrese
abstract: Entanglement asymmetry has emerged as a powerful probe of symmetry restoration and the quantum Mpemba effect. However, its conventional Rényi generalizations, defined as differences of Rényi entropies, are not monotones in the resource-theoretic sense. Here, we investigate an alternative family of asymmetry quantifiers based on sandwiched Rényi divergences, which satisfy monotonicity under symmetry-preserving quantum channels. Developing a two-parameter replica approach, we show how these quantities can be computed from charged moments and establish a remarkable correspondence with conventional Rényi asymmetries under the inversion of the Rényi index, $α\leftrightarrow 1/α$. This relation, exact for pure states, holds at leading order in the relevant scaling limits for homogeneous quantum quenches, including interacting integrable systems, and for Haar-random states. Applying these results to quenches from tilted ferromagnetic states, we demonstrate that the quantum Mpemba effect is remarkably robust, occurring throughout the entire family of sandwiched Rényi asymmetry monotones. We identify dynamical regimes in quenches from spatially inhomogeneous initial states where conventional Rényi asymmetries and genuine monotones exhibit qualitatively different behaviours. We also investigate a solvable toy model illustrating the possible dependence of Mpemba crossings on the Rényi index. Our findings establish a connection between conventional Rényi asymmetries and quantum resource theory, explaining their effectiveness in broad classes of nonequilibrium protocols while highlighting the additional information provided by genuine asymmetry monotones.

title: State convertibility in quantum-state texture from a general form of free operations
authors: Jose Alfredo de Leon
abstract: State convertibility specifies which transformations between states a quantum resource theory allows. In quantum-state texture, deterministic conversion criteria are known for qubits and pure sources in arbitrary dimension, but a general criterion for mixed states in higher dimensions is missing. We derive this exact criterion from a complete characterization of free operations in arbitrary finite dimension. Because the unique free state is pure, every free operation splits into a quantum filter and a residual completely positive map. Using this decomposition, we show that every allowed conversion admits a two-outcome measurement that retains the filtered state after one outcome and prepares a fixed state after the other. Conversion thus reduces to finding such a filter whose unnormalized output leaves a positive semidefinite remainder when subtracted from the target, a search we show to be solvable by semidefinite programming. Beyond deterministic conversion, the characterization of free operations can be used to study probabilistic and assisted manipulation of quantum-state texture. More broadly, since the construction relies on a pure fixed state, it also applies to other resource theories defined by free operations fixing such a state.

title: Simultaneous computation of multiple excited states via double bracket flows
authors: Reyhaneh Aghaei Saem, Mehrad Sahebi, Zoë Holmes, Yudai Suzuki
abstract: Efficient computation of excited states is essential for studying strongly correlated many-body systems and molecular electronic structure. In this work, we propose a framework for simultaneously simulating multiple excited states based on dynamical flows. The main idea is to exploit a common double bracket flow that drives different pure initial states toward different target excited states without such prior information. We establish a necessary condition for convergence and a sufficient condition for exponential convergence. We further develop two scheduling strategies: Chebyshev scheduling, which achieves optimal convergence near a fixed point but requires prior spectral information, and adaptive scheduling, which achieves comparable performance in numerical simulations without spectral information. Our results enable new classical and quantum algorithms for excited-state computation without prior preparation of lower-energy eigenstates.

title: Bound magic in multi-qubit systems
authors: Jonas Kitzinger, Jens Eisert, Ravi Kunjwal
abstract: Magic captures nonstabilizerness, a resource required for quantum computational speedups. We prove the existence of multi-qubit nonstabilizer states from which no pure magic can be distilled, even with arbitrarily many copies and rounds of stabilizer operations. Such bound magic states have previously been only known to exist in odd Hilbert-space dimensions, where positivity of discrete Wigner functions can be used analogously to the positive partial transpose (PPT) criterion for bound entanglement. We introduce a PPT analogue for magic in multi-qubit systems that is closed under tensor products and stabilizer operations and reduces to the stabilizer polytope for one and two qubits. This enables the proof of multi-qubit bound magic and the explicit construction of bound magic states for $n \geq 3$ qubits.

title: ProbFaS: Probabilistic Video Frame Selection for MLLMs via Multi-Fidelity Calibration
authors: Tianru Zhang, Mayank Nautiyal, Hugo Eidmann, Prashant Singh, Ekta Vats
abstract: Processing long videos with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is prohibitively expensive, making informative frame selection essential for accurate video understanding. The default uniform sampling often misses task-relevant keyframes, while recent training-free selectors instead pick frames by how well each one matches the question under an image-text alignment (ITA) score. However, we show that ITA signals correspond poorly with the MLLM's true needs: their rankings correlate weakly with downstream accuracy and are even negatively correlated on over 40% of questions, whereas the MLLM's internal yes/no judgment yields a much stronger signal. We present ProbFaS, a training- and label-free probabilistic pipeline that fuses both signals for key frame selection. ProbFaS treats dense ITA scores as cheap, biased measurements and sparse MLLM judgments as accurate, costly ones, unifying them via co-kriging, a multi-fidelity Gaussian process, to calibrate relevance across all frames. A temporal determinantal point process then selects frames capturing relevance peaks while preserving temporal coverage. Across Video-MME, MLVU and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS is the most accurate among fourteen state-of-the-art training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings (8-128 frames), outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 3.1 percentage points. On MLVU and LongVideoBench, 32 ProbFaS frames match or surpass the top baseline at 128 frames and uniform sampling with up to 768 frames.

title: Memory Is Not Ground Truth: Revising Navigation Authority under Unreliable VLM Evidence for Persistent Semantic Navigation
authors: Sumukh Shrote, Shenbagaraj Kannapiran, Eric Eaton, Camillo Jose Taylor
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable robots to reason about semantic and spatio-temporal context, verify task-relevant objects, and guide sensing and navigation. Persistent memory can reduce redundant search for field robots, but when should a memory continue to guide behavior? Repeated misses may suggest that a memory is stale. Our experiments show why this evidence can remain ambiguous under VLM-based perception. Using a Boston Dynamics Spot with four fixed cameras and a persistent spatio-temporal visual memory, we measure negative-verification behavior across targets, viewpoints, language queries, and repeated revisits. False-negative rates vary substantially across objects, nearby revisits often reproduce the same detector outcome, and some matched target-present and target-removed experiments yield identical miss histories. This ambiguity persists under changed observation geometry, identity-preserving query reformulation, and conditioning on a previously verified target image. These findings raise two questions: is the object still there, and is this memory still useful for navigation? We introduce a dependence-aware, reversible memory-update mechanism that avoids double-counting correlated misses and stops using unsupported memories as direct navigation goals without claiming that the object is absent. Later positive evidence can restore a memory's use for navigation. One resident onboard VLM is shared across memory verification, semantic frontier reasoning, and in-motion perception. In three matched real-robot decision contexts, an episode-local baseline selected a stale memory as its navigation objective in every case, whereas our method selected semantic frontiers in all three. A complementary trial re-verified the target during motion and promoted fresh memory. These results support revising memory actionability rather than interpreting failed detection as object absence.

title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
authors: Qihao Lin, Guanxu Chen, Shuhang Zheng, Xiaoya Lu, Jingyi Yang, Terumi Chiba, Wenyi Yu, Chao Zhang
abstract: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $μ$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $μ$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

title: One Ocean, Many Tasks: A Data-Grounded Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Marine Robotics
authors: Shuaijun Liu, Qifu Wen, Xingwei Chen, Xinwen Hu, Feiyang You, Sijia Chen, Ningxin Su
abstract: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. The suite supports multi-agent settings with 2-10 vehicles. Our simulator supports three to six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and produces standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests, enabling consistent aggregation across tasks, difficulties, and scaling settings. Experiments across dataset variants and scenes systematically stress planning and control under data-grounded disturbances and reveal trade-offs among heuristic baselines, Behavior Cloning (BC), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner.

title: Exact monogamy of steering and remote Wigner negativity for multimode Gaussian nodes
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty
abstract: Optical quantum networks route correlations through nodes that hold several modes and are linked to many neighbors. Steering is the correlation behind one-sided device-independent tasks and behind the remote preparation of non-Gaussian states. It is monogamous for a single mode, which can be steered by only one party, but how many neighbors can steer a node with $k$ modes was not known. We show that for Gaussian states the answer is exactly $2k-1$ when the neighbors use Gaussian measurements, with any number of measurement settings. The limit follows from a simple bound. To every neighbor we assign a share, computed from the covariance matrix, and we prove that the shares of all neighbors add up to at most $k$, irrespective of the amount of squeezing, amplification or noise the network contains. A neighbor steers the node by Gaussian measurements exactly when its share exceeds one half, and a network built from a harmonic tight frame reaches the limit. The same number governs remote Wigner negativity. A heralded non-Gaussian operation at the node can make at most $2k-1$ neighbors Wigner negative, and in our network a single heralded projection makes all of them negative in the same run. With $n$ settings of arbitrary measurements, at most $nk-1$ neighbors can steer the node or violate a Bell inequality with it. More than $2k-1$ neighbors can therefore steer the node or violate a Bell inequality with it only if they use non-Gaussian measurements with at least three settings, whereas entanglement can reach any number of neighbors. These results determine exactly how many neighbors one multimode node can serve with steering and with remote Wigner negativity.

title: Transition Path Sampling for Rare Events in Non-Markovian Open Quantum Systems
authors: Ritesh Pant, Kai Müller, Tarun Gera, Doran I. G. B. Raccah
abstract: Rare transitions govern the dynamics of many open quantum systems, but their probabilities and rates are difficult to calculate. Transition path sampling (TPS) of quantum systems has so far been limited to Markovian, perturbative descriptions. Here, we formulate TPS for non-Markovian quantum state diffusion, which is exact for Gaussian baths, extending it to non-Markovian and strongly coupled open quantum systems. For normal-to-superradiant tunneling in the unbalanced open Dicke model, we determine probabilities down to $10^{-8}$ and rates beyond the reach of brute force.

title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning
authors: Gaia Grosso, Sergio Rodriguez-Benitez, Louis Lyons
abstract: The look-elsewhere effect (LEE) arises when the location of an effect in parameter space is not specified in advance: scanning many locations inflates the significance of the largest excess, and the local $p$-value must be corrected into a global one. A well-established framework, rooted in the work of Davies and operationalised for particle physics by Gross and Vitells, provides this correction for scans over continuous parameters. Some aspects, however, remain unsettled. The definition of "elsewhere" is ambiguous and ranges from a single distribution to an entire experimental programme. Moreover, the analytical shortcuts of the classical framework do not carry over to searches based on machine learning (ML), which are affected by an implicit post-selection bias that depends on the model's resolution and expressiveness. This review covers the LEE in searches for new physics at colliders, from its statistical foundations to these modern challenges. We discuss the corrections for continuous scans and for multiple discrete tests, illustrated with simple numerical examples, and the interaction between ML and the LEE, which we connect to the broader literature on selective inference. We highlight open problems, including the computational cost of empirical calibration for complex models and the development of analytical shortcuts for ML test statistics, and offer recommendations for reporting discovery significance in both classical and ML-based searches in particle physics.

title: The Price of Quantum Advantage in Computational Chemistry
authors: Haejung Koh, Katerina Gratsea, Hao Zhang, Matthew Otten
abstract: As the fault-tolerant era approaches, the question shifts from ``is it possible'' to ``is it worthwhile.'' To assess practical quantum advantage against reliable classical baselines, we examine 26 benchmark instances including FeMoco, iron-sulfur clusters, cytochrome P450, and ruthenium catalysts using two selected configuration interaction solvers, SHCI and TrimCI. Comparing classical workloads with fault-tolerant resource estimates, we calculate the break-even whole-QPU hourly price. Even at an optimistic price of US\$7{,}000 per whole-QPU hour, and with mid-range CPU clusters, classical computation remains cheaper for six of seven systems. FeMoco alone remains sensitive to the classical method and extrapolation strategy. Wavefunction analysis further reveals how orbital choice affects the determinant support required for target-state overlap in quantum phase estimation (QPE). Our results highlight the importance of reliable classical references and trial-state characterization, and quantify the economic conditions under which quantum computing can become competitive with classical alternatives.

title: A comparison of two- and one-fluid dust solvers for dusty, supersonic turbulence
authors: Narges Vadood, Terrence S. Tricco
abstract: We model 3 and 10 $μ$m dust grains in supersonic, turbulent molecular cloud conditions to compare two different numerical methods solving dust coupled to gas through a drag term. One method models dust and gas as two separate species (two fluid) and the other the combination of dust and gas as a single mixture (one fluid) using the diffusion approximation. Simulations are performed in a 3D periodic box using the Phantom code. The gas probability distributions are consistent with a lognormal distribution for both methods and grain sizes. The dust distributions are different in the two methods, showing discrepancies particularly in regions of low density. The most significant difference between the two methods is in the dust-to-gas ratio distributions. Both methods peak at the mean dust-to-gas ratio of 0.01, but the two-fluid method has wider distributions than the one-fluid method suggesting excess dust concentration in dense filaments. Filaments are where the one-fluid method results are most accurate. The narrowing of the one-fluid distribution is also caused by the stopping time limiter used to maintain the terminal velocity approximation. This artificially makes the mixture more coupled in low-density regions. Our overall conclusion is that both methods are viable for the study of dust in molecular clouds, but that the correct method should be chosen based on the numerical Stokes number regime of the calculation to avoid numerical artifacts.

title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
authors: Rikard Vinge, Miguel A. Belenguer-Plomer, Isabelle Wittmann, Octavian Dumitru, Michele Lazzarini, Sergio Albani, Conrad M Albrecht
abstract:
This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios.
  Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .

title: Agentic LongLive: Asynchronous Agentic Memory for Long Video Generation
authors: Shaoteng Liu, Shuai Yang, Wei Huang, Luozhou Wang, Song Han, Yukang Chen
abstract: Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.

title: Cairn: Object-Centric 3D Trajectory Priors for Steering Frozen VLAs
authors: Agelos Kratimenos, Kostas Daniilidis, Evangelos Chatzipantazis
abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are capable low-level controllers, but they tie where objects go to the layouts they were trained on: when objects are moved or obstacles block the way, they carry them to the wrong place or into collisions. Fine-tuning on new layouts needs robot data for each one and erodes skills the model already has. We introduce Cairn, which keeps the VLA frozen and steers it at test time along learned 3D trajectories of the object in its gripper. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the held object, along with its pose when grasped and the instruction, and samples SE(3) trajectories up to its release that lead it around obstacles and turn it to fit through gaps. The prior and the VLA form the two levels of a hierarchical planner in which feedback runs both ways: the VLA's intended motion chooses and reshapes the trajectories, and the chosen one guides the VLA's denoising. Its predicted actions, mapped to the held object's poses through the grasp, are pulled toward the next waypoint, while the VLA's weights stay untouched. Across 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with displaced objects and obstacles, Cairn raises the success rate of a frozen π0.5 from 24.5% to 95.1%, above that of a π0.5 fine-tuned on our training layouts, without hurting standard LIBERO. On the third-party LIBERO-PRO benchmark, it raises success from 27.3% to 38.0%, and from 54.4% to 81.1% on the episodes it steers. On a real Franka, with a prior trained purely in simulation, it guides the frozen DROID π0.5 around an obstacle and to a placement at the limit of the arm's reach, where it otherwise fails. All code, models and data will be made public.

title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
authors: Lianghui Zhu, Shijie Wang, Xinggang Wang, Jinze Bai, Bo Wang, Xiang Bai
abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT

title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
authors: Lukas Aichberger, Adam Golinski, Arno Blaas, Arwen Bradley, Jacob Springer, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Michael Kirchhof, Sinead Williamson
abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
authors: Baihan Yang, Xin Lin, Yufan Wei, Baiang Li, Yuheng Liu, Juanxi Tian, Xiaohui Xie, Truong Nguyen
abstract: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https://white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/.

title: A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models
authors: Paul Vilars, Vincent Quoc-Huy Trinh, Maria Vakalopoulou, Dimitris Samaras, Stergios Christodoulidis, Mahdi S. Hosseini
abstract: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses.

title: MERLoc: Robust Robot Localization in Dynamic Environments with Pose-Based Retrieval over 3D Gaussian Splatting References
authors: Michael Baumgartner, Dario Mylonopoulos, Sammy Christen, Markus Gross, Moritz Bacher
abstract: Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present MERLoc, which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory. Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot's morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. Pre-encoding them for the chosen off-the-shelf localizer removes the reference encoder from inference. A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15-60 % in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion. The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz, enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects.

title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
authors: Charlie Griffin, Oliver Makins, Asa Cooper Stickland, Alessandro Abate, Yarin Gal, Abby D'Cruz, Xander Davies
abstract:
AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong.
  The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
authors: Xueyang Yu, Yifan Jing, Taiming Lu, Linrong Cai, Zhipeng Cai, Yunyang Xiong, Gabriel Sarch, Zhuang Liu
abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.

title: Neural Network Decoders For Qubit Loss
authors: J. Wilson Staples, Winston Fu, Yihe Dong, Jeff D. Thompson
abstract: Qubit loss is a significant source of error in many quantum hardware platforms, requiring circuits that periodically replace or reset qubits to maintain fault-tolerance. When the reset process includes loss-resolving measurements, this information can improve decoding and substantially reduce overhead compared to the case where this information is not available. Prior work has demonstrated loss-tolerant circuits for the surface code that show significantly improved thresholds and subthreshold scaling by incorporating loss information. However, the computational complexity of loss simulation and decoding, which falls outside of the usual stabilizer framework, has limited extending these studies to high-rate qLDPC codes, which are already challenging to decode in the absence of loss. In this work, we present a loss-aware convolutional neural-network (CNN) decoder framework that circumvents this challenge. Training is enabled by a novel sampler, \texttt{slim}, which achieves a throughput for circuits with Pauli noise and loss that is comparable to the state-of-the-art for pure Pauli noise. On the surface code with loss, the decoder matches the accuracy of computationally expensive most-likely error (MLE) decoders at much lower latency. For the $[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle (Gross) code, we study a walking syndrome extraction circuit with Pauli and loss errors. For physical error rates $p<1\%$, we observe a more than $10^3$-fold lower logical error rate for a pure loss model, relative to a pure Pauli error model at the same physical error rate, along with significantly enhanced sub-threshold error rate scaling. This demonstrates that loss-dominated error models can also significantly improve performance in a high-rate qLDPC code, and provides a simulation and decoder training platform that can be extended to other codes and algorithmic gadgets.

title: Massive Triangle in Cosmological Correlator beyond Conformal Coupling
authors: Taushif Ahmed, Syed Mehedi Hasan
abstract: A massive scalar coupled in pairs to the inflaton generates a one-loop primordial bispectrum whose mass corrections at generic momenta have lacked closed analytic expressions beyond conformal coupling. We obtain two leading mass corrections at arbitrary external momenta in terms of multiple polylogarithms of uniform weights three and four. Auxiliary-energy dressings preserve rational time integrals, revealing unexpected simplicity despite elliptic intermediate geometry. Independent full-loop evaluations, including blinded predictions, validate the closed forms. We also determine a subleading light-field singularity and recover the heavy-mass effective theory.

title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
